caption: The pathology report indicates that there is a tumor located in the left frontal lobe of the brain. The tumor is 10x8x4 cm in size and has a soft, brown-white surface with moderate margins. Microscopically, the tumor shows loose architecture and infiltrates the surrounding benign brain tissue. It is composed of groups of gemiscytes and spindle cells, with elongated and irregular nuclei that are hyperchromatic and have small nucleoli. Mitotic figures are present, indicating active cell division. The tumor also has a fibrillar background and hyperplastic blood vessels. It is necrotic and shows hemorrhage and invasion of lymphocytes. The diagnosis is Astrocytoma, grade I. No additional comments are provided.

The pathology report describes a brain tumor in a 59-year-old male that was diagnosed as an Anaplastic Gemistocytic Astrocytoma (WHO Grade II). The report mentions the clinical history of the patient having a seizure and imaging showing an abnormal region of the brain with discontinuous enhancement in the left temporal lobe. The gross examination describes the tissue received for analysis. The microscopic examination reveals infiltration of the brain by a glial neoplasm characterized by cellular pleomorphism, including prominent gemistocytes, perivascular lymphocytic inflammation, and scattered mitotic figures. Immunohistochemical findings are also reported, including GFAP highlighting tumor cells, HANS6 not demonstrating a macrophage infiltrate, and a Ki-67 labeling index of 38. FISH interpretation reveals polysomy of chromosome 7 centromere and EGFR, intact chromosome 10 centromere and PTEN, and loss of SP21 and chromosome 9 centromere. The report also mentions a multivariate survival analysis showing a lower hazard of short survival in patients with 0-2 abnormal markers compared to those with >2 markers. Additional immunohistochemical labeling indexes indicate positivity for Leukocyte Common Antigen (LCA), EGF receptor (EGFR), AKT, and MAPK, and negativity for Carbonic Anhydrase IX and VEGF. The report is certified by the pathologist who conducted the evaluation.

2. Right adrenal gland, benign adrenal gland (from the additional tissue).

The pathologist has personally examined and interpreted the slides from this case.

Summary:
The pathology report describes a case of an adrenal mass with a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. The tumor showed capsular invasion, and vascular invasion couldn't be ruled out. Immunostains were positive for chromogranin, synaptophysin, and S-100. The report also mentions that the laboratory performing the tests is certified under CLIA for high complexity testing. The gross description of the specimen indicates a pink/red soft tissue mass with a central cyst and a yellowish fibrous wall. A portion of the tumor and a small piece of uninvolved adrenal tissue were procured for further testing.

This pathology report describes the findings of a surgical pathology examination of specimens from a patient. The report includes the following diagnoses:

1. Left omental mass: Fat necrosis
2. Spleen resection: Low grade B cell Lymphoma with CDS expression. A hematopathologist noted atypical lymphoid cells in the red pulp of the spleen, positive for CD20 and CD23. The cells were negative for cyclinD1 and IgD. The diagnosis favored a low grade B cell lymphoma, with differential diagnoses including splenic marginal zone lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL), and mantle cell lymphoma.
3. Left adrenal gland resection: Pheochromocytoma with involvement of adipose tissue by low grade B cell lymphoma.

The report also mentions that immunohistochemistry and in-situ hybridization tests were performed for diagnosis, and that the Laboratory of Pathology developed and determined the performance characteristics of these tests.

The clinical history indicates that the patient had an adrenal mass and a previous biopsy of surrounding retroperitoneal lymph nodes consistent with B cell lymphoma.

The gross description notes the submission of three specimens: left omental mass, spleen, and left adrenal gland. The spleen specimen had a small area of atypical cells in the red pulp and prominent white pulp.

The report concludes by stating that the remaining specimen was submitted for permanent processing and that the report should not be filed in the patient's medical record.

The pathology report describes an adrenal tumor that is ovoid and encapsulated, weighing 83g and measuring 65x60x45mm. The tumor appears dark red and has pseudocystic cavities filled with blood. 

Microscopically, the tumor is solid and alveolar in shape with extensive hemorrhagic necrosis. There are areas of adrenal cortex remnants at the periphery of the tumor. Focal cytologic atypias are observed within the tumor. 

Staining for $100 protein is positive in sustentacular cells and nervous fibers. Chromogranin staining is positive in pheochromocytoma cells but negative in adrenal cortex remnants. Alpha-inhibin staining is negative in pheochromocytoma cells and positive in adrenal cortex remnants. MIB 1 staining shows less than 1% of positive nuclei. 

Other findings include large nests or diffuse growth (>10% of tumor volume) on PAS staining, central or confluent tumor necrosis, high cellularity, cellular monotony, tumor cell spindling (even if focal), mitotic figures greater than 3/10 high power fields, atypical mitotic figures, extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, capsular invasion, profound nuclear pleomorphism, and nuclear hyperchromasia. 

The report does not include information about the procurement and confirmation dates.

Based on the pathology report, it appears that the patient had a right adrenal pheochromocytoma, which was surgically removed through a laparoscopic adrenalectomy. The specimen received for examination was a 4.8 x 3.1 x up to 3.1 cm brown-tan, indurated mass that appeared grossly free/encapsulated. The mass was found to arise from the adrenal gland itself. The final diagnosis confirmed the presence of a 6.8 cm pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland.

The pathology report summarizes the findings of the examination of multiple specimens. The main findings are as follows:

A. LEFT KIDNEY AND ADRENAL TUMOR:
- The specimen consists of a kidney and adrenal tumor.
- The tumor is a malignant pheochromocytoma, involving the adrenal medulla and extending to the peri-adrenal adipose tissue.
- Lymphovascular invasion is identified.
- Surgical resection margins are negative for pheochromocytoma.
- The kidney is negative for tumor.

B. SPLENIC LESION:
- The specimen consists of a biopsy of a splenic mesothelial cyst.

C. PERIAORTIC LYMPH NODES:
- The specimen consists of resected peri-aortic lymph nodes.
- One of the twelve lymph nodes shows metastatic pheochromocytoma.

Note: The malignant pheochromocytoma in the adrenal gland shows various histologic features and involves the peri-adrenal adipose tissue, infiltrating into lymphatic vessels and blood vessels. The tumor is positive for Chromogranin A, Synaptophysin, and S100, but negative for EMA. Ki67 marks approximately ...% of tumor cells.

The pathology report describes a case of a pheochromocytoma, which is a tumor of the adrenal gland. The patient has a history of hypertension and diabetes. The tumor is highly vascularized and measures 5.5 cm in size. The tumor cells are large with polygonal and moderately eosinophilic cytoplasm. There is an increase in cellular density in some areas with smaller cells. No necrosis or mitotic activity is observed. The tumor is confined within a fibrous capsule but shows infiltration of the capsule and presence of vascular invasion. The rest of the adrenal gland appears normal.

The pathology report describes a surgical pathology consultation for a patient named rciont who had a left adrenal pheochromocytoma. The gross description states that the adrenal gland is distorted by a tumor measuring 6.5 x 6.5 x 4.2 cm. The tumor is dusky and hemorrhagic with a cyst filled with bloody fluid. A pigmented area is also present. Microscopic examination reveals a dominant lesion of the adrenal tumor with solid nesting architecture. The cells have indistinct borders, abundant basophilic cytoplasm, and focal nuclear pleomorphism. Degenerative changes such as hemorrhage, cystic change, and fatty degeneration are noted. The tumor has an incomplete capsule without frank invasion. No extra-adrenal invasion, involvement of resection margins, lymphovascular involvement, or other adrenal pathology is identified. No lymph nodes are identified.

The pathology report describes the findings from various tissue specimens obtained during surgery for a retroperitoneal mass. Here are the key details:

1. Soft tissue, peritoneum: The excised tissue consists of loose fibroconnective tissue and fragments of adipose tissue.
2. Lymph node, aortocaval (below renal vein): This excised lymph node shows hyperplasia with vascular medullary accentuation.
3. Lymph node, aortocaval: This excised lymph node is benign.
4. Kidney and adrenal gland, right: A perirenal mass consistent with pheochromocytoma is found, measuring 10 x 5 x 5 cm. The tumor mass is adjacent to, but not involving, the adrenal gland. Some features suggest malignant pheochromocytoma, including tumor size and perforation into the renal vein. Immunohistochemical studies were performed, and the neoplastic cells are negative for some markers (AE 1/3, CAMS, HMB-45, MART-1) and positive for others (synaptophysin, chromogranin, melan A, inhibin). S-100 staining is negative for neoplastic cells but positive for reticuloendothelial cells. Continued clinical evaluation for bone metastases is recommended.

Overall, the report confirms the diagnosis of a pheochromocytoma in the right kidney and provides additional information about the lymph nodes and peritoneum. The tumor has some features suggestive of malignancy, and further evaluation is needed.

The pathology report describes a 55x45x35 mm, 50g pheochromocytoma tumor that is enclosed in a thin fibrous capsule. The tumor is grey-red in color with focal hemorrhages. Microscopically, it is solid and alveolar in shape with some areas of hemorrhage. There is a rim of adrenocortical tissue around the periphery. The tumor does not invade the adrenal capsule or surrounding adipose tissue. There is sporadic nuclear hyperchromasia, but no regular or atypical mitoses or necroses. Staining for $100 protein is weakly to moderately positive in pheochromocytoma cells and strongly positive in sustentacular cells. MIBI staining is less than 1% positive. The tumor is classified as PASS, indicating no evidence of malignancy. There are no large nests or diffuse growth, necrosis, extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, capsular invasion, or profound nuclear pleomorphism. The tumor has high cellularity, cellular monotony, and some spindling. The presence of mitotic figures and atypical mitoses is noted. The procurement and confirmation dates are not provided in the summary.

Pathology Report Summary:

The report describes the findings of a tumor in the left adrenal gland. The tumor was well circumscribed, measuring 2.6x2.5x2em, and was completely removed through surgery. Microscopically, the tumor showed an alveolar growth pattern with cells of middle or large size. These cells had eosinophilic, granular, and bright cytoplasm with eccentric nuclei and well-recognizable nucleoli. Some cells had eosinophilic nuclear inclusion bodies, PAS-positive inclusions, and brownish pigment. There were no atypical mitoses or highly atypical nuclei. No tumor cells were found in blood vessels or in the periphery of the adrenal gland. The tumor showed a high degree of vasculature. Immunohistochemical testing showed positivity for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, vimentin, and protein 100, with a Ki67 index of less than 1%. There was no nuclear staining for keratin, LuS, and p53. Based on these findings, the diagnosis is pheochromocytoma of the left adrenal gland (PD-6-3).

The pathology report states that a 1-year-old female patient underwent a C-section and developed cardiogenic shock afterwards. Lab work-up showed the presence of a pheochromocytoma. The patient underwent a left adrenalectomy, and the pathology report confirms the presence of a pheochromocytoma in the left adrenal gland.

The pathology report indicates that a left adrenal mass was removed from the patient. The mass measured 11 x 9.8 x 7.5 cm and had a cystic, tan-brown appearance with red hemorrhagic fluid. The surrounding adrenal gland appeared normal. The diagnosis is pheochromocytoma, which is a tumor of the adrenal gland that produces hormones. The tumor measured 8.0 x 4.5 x 4.0 cm and showed invasion into the capsule and lymphovascular spaces. There were 1 to 2 mitotic figures per 10 high power fields, indicating some cell division. The tumor also displayed moderate nuclear pleomorphism and diffuse growth pattern, as well as extension into adjacent adipose tissue. It is noted that the tumor margin was <0.1 cm from the inked surgical margin. Immunohistochemistry and special stains were performed, indicating positivity for MIBI-Ki67, chromogranin A, and synaptophysin. The report also mentions that the interpretation of these results was guided by published literature and internal review, and that the tests used were not cleared or approved by the FDA.

The pathology report describes a surgical procedure called an adrenalectomy, in which the right adrenal gland was removed. The specimen consisted of a well-encapsulated soft mass with a yellow color and some areas of bleeding. The size of the mass was 7.5 x 5.4 x 6.7 cm. A thin strip of normal adrenal gland tissue was identified at one edge of the mass. The capsule of the mass was marked with black ink. Representative sections of the mass were taken for further examination. The final diagnosis of the specimen was a pheochromocytome, and the margins were negative for any abnormality.

This pathology report describes the findings of a surgical procedure in which various tissues were examined. The main findings are as follows:

1. Left adrenal gland adrenalectomy: Pheochromocytoma present, with adjacent adrenal cortex showing thickening suggestive of hyperplasia.

2. Left lobe and right lobe of the thyroid: Colloid nodular disease present.

3. Biopsy of a nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid: Benign reactive lymph node, no tumor seen.

4. Thymus: Both the right and left thymus tissue are unremarkable.

Immunostaining tests showed that the lesional cells from the adrenal gland are positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin. Sustentacular cells were also stained. It is noted that the immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests performed have not been cleared or approved by the FDA but the laboratory is certified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing.

The clinical information indicates that the procedure was performed to investigate an adrenal nodule consistent with pheochromocytoma, large multinodular goiters, and hyperparathyroidism.

Specimens submitted include the left adrenal gland, left lobe and right lobe of the thyroid, a nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid, and thymus tissues.

The gross description of the specimens indicates the size, weight, and appearance of each tissue.

In summary, the pathology report confirms the presence of a pheochromocytoma in the left adrenal gland, colloid nodular disease in both lobes of the thyroid, and a benign reactive lymph node in a nodule within the right lobe of the thyroid. The thymus tissues are found to be unremarkable. Further immunostaining tests were performed on the lesional cells from the adrenal gland.

The pathology report describes the findings from the surgical removal of the right adrenal gland. The specimen consisted of a 60g adrenal gland with a well-circumscribed mass measuring 3.9 x 3.3 x 3.0 cm. The mass had a tan, glistening rubbery cut surface with multiple hemorrhagic foci. It was uncertain whether the mass originated from the cortical surface of the gland. The remaining adrenal gland appeared normal. The microscopic analysis confirmed the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma, supported by positive immunohistochemical staining for chromogranin, synaptophysin, and calretinin. Other immunostains were negative. The report also mentioned the possibility of malignancy in pheochromocytomas, although there were no definitive features to confirm malignancy in this case. Further discussions with the healthcare provider were recommended for any questions or concerns.

The pathology report describes a surgical procedure performed on a 60-year-old female with a pheochromocytoma. The procedure involved a left posterior approach for a retroperitoneal adrenalectomy. The removed adrenal gland measured 8.0 x 4.5 x 6.0 cm and contained a 4.5 x 4.0 x 3.0 cm encapsulated mass. The mass was partially solid and cystic with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. The report confirms the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma and states that the margins were negative.

The pathology report describes a retroperitoneal mass and right adrenal gland that were surgically resected. The mass was identified as an extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglioma, with a maximum tumor size of 3.3 cm. The margins were negative, indicating that the tumor was fully removed. The adrenal gland itself was benign. Special stains confirmed the diagnosis, showing positive results for synaptophysin and chromogranin, and highlighting an intact sustentacular cell network. The histologic examination of the tumor indicated a low-grade neoplasm with a typical paraganglioma pattern and no definite malignant features.

The pathology report indicates that the specimen labeled "interaortocaval tumor" is a pheochromocytoma measuring 5.5 x 4 x 3.5 cm. The inked surgical margins are free of tumor, and no tumor is seen in one lymph node. However, no adrenal tissue was identified. The gross description states that the specimen is a single piece of red/purple, soft tissue with a smooth surface. The cut surface is homogenous, soft, and dark purple, with a section procured for further analysis. The specimen has been sampled generously and representative sections have been submitted.

The pathology report describes the findings of a surgical pathology examination of a specimen taken from the right adrenal gland. The diagnosis is pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal gland. The tumor cells are positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin, and the MIB-1 immunostain demonstrates a low proliferation index. The report also mentions that immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests were performed for diagnosis, and the laboratory is certified under the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988 (CLIA) to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing. The report includes a gross description of the specimen and mentions that a portion of the tissue was procured for research. Overall, the report confirms the presence of a pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland.

The pathology report reveals the following findings:

- The specimen received is a 46.2 gram adrenal gland with attached adipose tissue.
- The adrenal gland measures 10.5 x 5.5 x 1.5 cm and has a well encapsulated 1.8 cm nodule.
- The adrenal nodule is composed of clear cells resembling zona fasciculata cells, consistent with adrenal cortical adenoma.
- There is also a 2.2 cm nodule within the adjacent adipose tissue.
- The nodule in the adipose tissue is composed of nests and trabeculae of cells with abundant granular cytoplasm and round nuclei, surrounded by a rich vascular network.
- Immunohistochemistry stains for Synaptophysin and Chromogranin are positive in the tumor cells, while S-100 protein highlights the sustentacular cell network.
- There is no evidence of increased mitoses, necrosis, or vascular or capsular invasion in either nodule.

It is important to note that the report mentions that the immunohistochemistry test used has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, but the pathologist certifies that positive and negative controls were reviewed and approved.

The pathology report describes a surgical specimen of a right adrenal gland with a pheochromocytoma, a tumor measuring 5.5 cm. The tumor cells are arranged in nests and have a granular cytoplasm. The nuclei of the tumor cells are oval with prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemical staining shows that the tumor cells stain positive for synaptophysin, while the sustentacular cells stain positive for S-100. The adrenal cortex tissue is unremarkable. The gross description states that the specimen measures 4.5 x 4.3 x 4.8 cm and weighs 62.0 grams. A portion of the tumor and normal adrenal gland are procured for research purposes, and the remaining specimen is sent for permanent processing.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the right adrenal gland. The tumor is red and light tan in color and measures 2.1 cm in diameter. Microscopically, the tumor is composed of medium-sized cells with enlarged nuclei, chromatin, and prominent nucleoli. Some cells display more pronounced changes in cell morphology and enlarged nuclei. The tumor is well separated from surrounding tissue by a fibrous capsule. Hyaline globules are observed within some cells. There is no significant increase in mitotic activity, no evidence of necrosis, vessel invasion, or capsule destruction. The reported PASS Score for this tumor is 1 out of a maximum of 20, indicating a low likelihood of malignancy. The final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma.

The pathology report describes the findings from a left adrenal gland specimen. The macroscopy reveals a tumor measuring 4.5 x 5 x 4 cm with cystic defects, hemorrhage, and calcification. The tumor is completely encapsulated and presents near the resection plane. Microscopy shows normal adrenal tissue along with a fibrous capsule surrounding the tumor, which consists of polymorphic round or angular nuclei with granular chromatin and eosinophilic cytoplasm. There are also polynuclear tumor cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and areas of dilated capillaries, hemorrhage, and fibrosis. The tumor infiltrates the adjacent fat but does not show angio-invasion, necrosis, or mitoses. The preliminary conclusion is that the left adrenal tumor is a pheochromocytoma measuring up to 4 cm in diameter, completely removed with a minimum margin of 1 mm. There is also noted infiltration of surrounding adipose tissue.

The pathology report indicates that a laparoscopic adrenalectomy was performed on the left adrenal gland. The adrenal gland weighed 112 grams and had a spherical lesion with a diameter of 45 mm. There was also an iatrogenic lesion (less than 10 mm) in the normal adrenal tissue. The adrenal gland had adherent fatty tissues and the preparation was already largely halved. The largest lesion had a diameter of 4.3 cm and a golden-brown discoloration. There was another lesion with a diameter of 1.3 cm on the opposite end. Between the two lesions, there was pre-existing adrenal tissue measuring 1.7 x 1.7 cm. Microscopically, the tumor consisted of solid fields with some "Zelbalien" configuration. The tumor cells had finely granular cytoplasm with hyaline inclusions and large nuclei with polymorphic vesicular chromatin pattern. There were no mitoses, necrosis, or vascular ingrowth. The tumor was completely removed and surrounded by a capsule without capsular invasion. Additionally, there was nodular hyperplasia of the pre-existing adrenal cortex. Further research showed positive cytoplasmic chromogranin and inhibin in the pre-existent adrenal cortex, but negative in the tumor cells. S100 was positive in sustentaculair cells. The conclusion of the report is that a pheochromocytoma measuring up to 4.3 cm was completely removed through the laparoscopic excision of the left adrenal gland. There was also nodular hyperplastic changes in the pre-existing adrenal cortex with a macroscopic nodule of 1.4 cm.

The pathology report describes a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland. The report notes areas suspicious for vascular invasion. Immunohistochemical studies show positive staining for chromogranin and synaptophysin, focal positivity for P53, and negative staining for c-Kit. The tumor has an intermediate proliferative index. The report mentions that the laboratory is certified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing. The pre-operative and post-operative diagnoses were the same, which was pheochromocytoma. The gross description of the specimen includes the size, weight, and appearance of the adrenal gland and the presence of a solitary nodule in the medulla. Sections of the specimen were submitted for further testing and analysis. The report includes the signature of a resident and a request not to file it in the medical record.

The pathology report describes the findings of an adrenal tumor that was removed surgically. The tumor is identified as multiple pheochromocytomas, with at least four separate nodules ranging in size from 0.8 to 2.5 cm. Three of the nodules are entirely within the adrenal gland, while the fourth partially extends beyond the adrenal capsule. The nodules vary in appearance, suggesting separate neoplasms rather than a single tumor. The report notes the absence of adrenal medullary hyperplasia, soft tissue invasion, vascular invasion, or necrosis. Mitoses (cell division) are not identified. Immunohistochemical staining for Ki-67 (a marker of cell proliferation) is low overall, with occasional hot spots. Other immunohistochemical markers tested include calcitonin (negative), S100 (variable numbers of stained cells), neurofilament (rare positive cells), and SDHB (positive tumor cells indicating normal succinate dehydrogenase genes). The report suggests the possibility of a hereditary tumor syndrome, most likely MEN2, and recommends further clinical-pathological correlation. The gross description of the surgical specimen confirms the presence of multiple separate nodules within the adrenal gland.

The pathology report indicates the following findings:

A. Left adrenal, adrenalectomy:
- Pheochromocytoma present, with no evidence of capsular or vascular invasion by tumor.

B. Right adrenal, adrenalectomy:
- Pheochromocytoma present, with no evidence of capsular or vascular invasion by tumor.

C. Possible parathyroid:
- Small fragment of parathyroid tissue present.

D. Left levels 3 and 4, lymph nodes:
- 1 out of 13 lymph nodes involved with metastatic tumor.

E. Thyroid and level 6 contents, total thyroidectomy:
- Medullary thyroid carcinoma present bilaterally, with foci of nodular c-cell hyperplasia.
- Enlarged parathyroid gland consistent with parathyroid adenoma.
- No lymph node involvement.

F. Right levels 3 and 4, lymph nodes:
- No lymph node involvement.

Tumor Characteristics:

- Total thyroidectomy performed.
- Medullary thyroid carcinoma present in both lobes.
- Tumor size: 3.2 cm.
- Margins uninvolved by carcinoma.
- No lymph-vascular invasion or extrathyroidal extension identified.
- Stage: pT2 (tumor more than 2 cm, limited to thyroid).
- Regional lymph node metastasis: pN1b (metastases to unilateral, bilateral or contralateral cervical or superior mediastinal lymph nodes), with 1 out of 25 lymph nodes involved.
- Distant metastasis cannot be assessed (pMX).
- No additional pathologic findings identified.

Gross Findings:

- Left adrenal: 244 gram mass with tan-yellow encapsulated tumor.
- Right adrenal: 54 gram encapsulated mass with tan-brown to orange appearance.
- Parathyroid: small tan-yellow tissue fragment.
- Left levels 3 and 4 lymph nodes: 8.0 cm fibrofatty tissue with palpable nodules.
- Thyroid and level 6 contents: intact thyroid with attached fibroadipose tissue and parathyroid candidate.

This pathology report describes the findings of a left adrenal gland specimen. The macroscopic findings indicate the presence of a tumor surrounded by a fatty-connective tissue capsule with a partially cystic appearance and hemorrhage. The microscopic findings show that the tumor tissue consists of polygonal cells with granular cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei. The stroma is vascularized, and the tumor is surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. Normal adrenal tissue is also present in the specimen. The lymphatic vessels show invasion by tumor cells. The diagnosis is pheochromocytoma of the left adrenal gland with lymphatic invasion. A separate pathology report mentions the diagnosis of a lymph node metastasis, which was removed during the initial surgery.

The pathology report describes a case involving a left adrenal pheochromocytoma. This is a tumor of the adrenal gland, measuring 3.0 cm. The tumor does not show any signs of increased mitotic activity, vascular invasion, necrosis, or nuclear pleomorphism. The PASS (Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal Gland Scaled Score) score is 0, indicating a low likelihood of malignancy. The gross description of the specimen confirms the presence of a rounded mass within the left adrenal gland, with a staple line on one end. The mass is described as pale, well-circumscribed, yellow-tan, and hemorrhagic. A portion of the mass is submitted to the tumor bank for further analysis. The report also mentions the submission of the uninvolved adrenal gland for analysis.

This pathology report describes a case of a 90-year-old patient with a history of pheochromocytomas and hypertension. The report indicates that the patient underwent a left adrenalectomy, and the specimen received for analysis was a fresh adrenal gland that had been previously bisected. The weight and measurements of the gland are provided. The report notes the presence of a tumor in the adrenal gland, which is described as encapsulated and exhibiting brown hemorrhagic features. There is no evidence of necrosis. The report confirms the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma in the left adrenal gland.

The pathology report describes the findings from a right adrenalectomy, resection of a paraganglioma, and a periaortic-pericave lymph node. The patient presented with a history of headache, hypertension, and right abdominal pain. Imaging revealed two hypervascular retroperitoneal nodules and high levels of metanephrines. The patient also had preeclampsia during pregnancy and gave birth to a healthy child. The report includes details about the macroscopy and microscopy of the tumors and lymph node. The adrenal tumor is composed of small cells with high cellularity and nuclear atypia. The interstitial tissue is reduced and there are visible hemorrhagic suffusions. The periaortic-pericave paraganglioma consists of small pheochromocytomic cells arranged in different patterns. Hemorrhagic reorganizations are visible and the tumor invades surrounding tissues and a lymph node. Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for chromogranin and synaptophysin. The conclusion states that the prognosis of these chromaffin tumors appears reserved.

The pathology report indicates the following findings:

- Diagnosis: Extra-adrenal paraganglioma measuring 4.4cm in soft tissue para-adrenal location.
- No pathological diagnosis was made for the adrenal gland.
- The adrenal gland is intact and shows no evidence of medullary hyperplasia.
- The paraganglioma is not connected with or involving the adrenal.
- The specimen container contains an adrenalectomy specimen weighing 78.3g and measuring 10.8 x 7.5 x 3cm.
- The adrenal gland with the mass measures 6 x 3 x 0.7cm.
- Surrounding yellow adipose tissue is 0.2 to 2.0cm thick, with a thin layer of fascia measuring 9.0 x 3.5cm.
- The mass is thinly encapsulated, coarsely lobulated, measuring 4.4 x 4.0 x 3.0cm, with a shiny, bulging, golden-brown cut surface and focal black discoloration.
- The mass is not directly connected to the adrenal gland.
- The adrenal gland appears normal.
- No other nodules or lymph nodes were identified in the surrounding fat.
- Sections of tumor and normal adrenal were frozen for tumor banking.
- The remainder of the specimen was submitted for further analysis.

The pathology report indicates that the patient had a laparoscopic adrenalectomy to remove a tumor from the left adrenal gland. The tumor is diagnosed as a pheochromocytoma measuring 15.0 cm in greatest dimension. The surgical margin of resection is negative for tumor. Additionally, there is invasion of the peri-adrenal soft tissue and involvement of a large vein wall. Nuclear pleomorphism and vascular invasion are present. The Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score (PASS) for the tumor is 7, indicating a potential for malignant behavior. Clinical follow-up is advised. The report has been reviewed and confirmed by another pathologist. The specimen submitted consists of the pheochromocytoma and peri-adrenal soft tissue. A gross description is provided for each specimen.

Summary of Pathology Report:

The pathology report describes a specimen labeled "right adrenal" which was received as a 13.0 x 10.5 x 2.5 cm portion of disrupted yellow-red lobulated fibroadipose tissue. Within this disrupted area is a 7.5 x 3.5 x 3.0 cm adrenal gland. The adrenal gland contains a 4.0 x 3.0 x 3.0 cm mass. The capsule of the mass is stripped due to the disruption of the tissue. The mass exhibits a rough orange-yellow rim with a soft red-brown partially cystic center. The uninvolved adrenal exhibits a thin orange-tan cortical rim and a central tan-brown medulla. The weight of the gland is 50.1 g. A histological examination has been performed on the specimen, and there are no charge codes associated with the case.

This pathology report describes the findings from a surgical consultation on a patient named Acossons who underwent a right adrenalectomy for a suspected pheochromocytoma. The gross description of the adrenal gland indicates that there are two masses present - a small yellow nodule measuring 0.7 x 0.6 x 0.6 cm and a larger red-brown nodule measuring 2.1 x 2.0 x 1.6 cm. The remaining adrenal tissue shows a variegated appearance with smaller yellow areas. No abnormalities are noted in the surrounding fatty tissue. Representative sections of the masses and adrenal tissue have been stored frozen and submitted for further analysis.

The pathology report describes a right adrenal tumor that measures 75x60x30 mm and weighs 96.8 grams. The tumor has a soft consistency with a central white scar. There are also areas of non-tumoral adrenal tissue with atrophy. Microscopically, the tumor is described as a pheochromocytoma with solid, alveolar, and diffuse growth patterns. There are focal areas of hemorrhage and the tumor cells appear polygonal and atrophied. Some spindle-formed cells are also present. There is no evidence of angioinvasion. Immunohistochemistry testing shows sporadic staining for S100 protein and less than 2% of cells expressing MIB 1. 

The tumor meets several criteria for malignancy, including the presence of large nests or diffuse growth, tumor necrosis, high cellularity, cellular monotony, tumor cell spindling, and mitotic figures. It does not show features of extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, capsular invasion, profound nuclear pleomorphism, or nuclear hyperchromasia. These findings lead to a diagnosis of a low-grade pheochromocytoma. The report does not include the procurement or confirmation dates.

The pathology report describes the diagnosis and findings of a patient with a presumptive pheochromocytoma. The report states that a neoplasm consistent with paraganglioma was found in the paraspinal tumor and deep margin, with negative margins. Immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests were performed and confirmed the diagnosis. The report also mentions the submission of three separate specimens for analysis: lateral and medial margins, as well as the paraspinal tumor. Gross descriptions of the specimens are provided.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the right adrenal gland. The tumor weighs 12 g and has a grey-brown color with a smooth surface and fibrous capsule. Microscopically, the tumor is composed of polygonal and spindle cells arranged in solid and alveolar patterns. There are also small remnants of the adrenal cortex and proliferation of adrenal cortex cells in the capsule. The tumor shows polymorphic features with hyperchromatic nuclei in some areas. Plasmatic cells are present in dense infiltration, and staining for kappa and lambda light chains is positive, suggesting a polyclonal origin. Sustentacular cells are seen in the well-differentiated parts of the tumor. Approximately 2-3% of tumor cells show positive staining for the MIB-1 marker. Staining for chromogranin is positive in large tumor cells but negative in adrenal cortex remnants and periadrenal adipose tissue. Additionally, smaller cells behind the adrenal capsule show positive staining, indicating possible extracapsular tumor proliferation in adipose tissue. No angioinvasion is observed. The report also lists various features of the tumor, including diffuse growth, tumor necrosis, high cellularity, cellular monotony, spindling of tumor cells, mitotic figures, atypical mitotic figures, extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, capsular invasion, profound nuclear pleomorphism, and nuclear hyperchromasia. The total number of mentioned features is 8. The report does not provide information on the procurement date or confirmation date.

The pathology report indicates that a partial adrenalectomy was performed on the right adrenal gland due to a pheochromocytoma. The tumor cells were positive for Synaptophysin and chromogranin, as determined by immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests. The report states that the laboratory is certified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing. The gross description of the specimen indicates that a portion of the adrenal gland with attached fat was received, weighing 5 grams and measuring 40x2.4x1.6 cm. There was a well-circumscribed and medullary nodule present within the adrenal gland, measuring 2.1x1.8x1.5 cm. The nodule was orange-red in color and soft in consistency. Approximately 50% of tissue from the center of the nodule and 40% of normal adrenal gland tissue were procured for further testing. The remaining specimen was submitted for permanent processing. The final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma.

The pathology report confirms the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal gland. There is no evidence of invasion into surrounding structures. Immunostaining tests were performed and support the diagnosis. The laboratory is certified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing. The gross description of the specimen is provided, including its weight, measurements, and associated adipose tissue. Cassettes of representative tumor and normal adrenal gland sections are submitted for permanent processing. The report is signed and dated by a resident. The final result is the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma.

This pathology report summarizes findings from various biopsies and a surgical excision. The patient has metastatic paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma, a type of endocrine tumor. The tumor has spread to multiple lymph nodes, with extranodal extension and involvement of adjacent tissues including the kidney, adrenal gland, pancreas, spleen, and stomach. The tumor shows characteristics of paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma on immunohistochemical staining. The exact site of origin is difficult to determine, but it is considered malignant based on the presence of metastatic disease. The tumor is categorized as pT4, pN1 according to the AJCC staging system.

This pathology report describes a left neck tumor diagnosed as a paraganglioma. The tumor cells show strong immunoreactivity for synaptophysin and chromogranin. Microscopic examination reveals nests and small lobules of neoplastic cells with neuroendocrine features. The cells have round to oval nuclei, speckled chromatin, and weakly eosinophilic cytoplasm. Cytologic atypia is mild, and mitotic figures are rare. The tumor is invested by hyalinized stroma and is adjacent to a network of vascular structures. Necrosis is not present. Overall, the histologic features are consistent with a paraganglioma.

Summary:

The pathology report refers to a case of a patient with a pheochromocytoma, a type of tumor found in the right adrenal gland. The tumor measures 6.2 cm in its greatest dimension. The specimen is intact and measures 6.9 x 5.2 x 3.1 cm. There are no signs of invasion into the capsule, extra-adrenal tissues, lymphovascular, or blood vascular structures. Surgical margins are negative and the adrenal gland away from the tumor appears normal. No lymph nodes are involved. The gross description of the specimen confirms the presence of a tan/brown soft cystic mass originating from the adrenal gland's medulla. The mass occupies a significant portion of the resection. Sections of the mass and uninvolved adrenal tissue are submitted for further examination.

Summary: The pathology report states that the patient, a female with a history of pheochromocytoma, underwent a right adrenalectomy to remove a right adrenal mass. The specimen received was a 5 x 4.5 x 3.5 cm section of adrenal gland with a circumscribed mass weighing 32 grams. The mass had a gray/pink hemorrhagic cut surface. A section of grossly normal adrenal gland and three fragments of normal rib bone were also submitted. An intraoperative consultation provided a preliminary diagnosis of neuroendocrine tumor. The report emphasizes not to file this information in the patient's medical record.

The pathology report describes a surgical biopsy of a right adrenal tumor, which was found to be a pheochromocytoma. Staining for chromogranin and synaptophysin was positive. Various sections of normal adrenal tissue and nodules were submitted for permanent processing. No other significant findings were mentioned in the report.

The pathology report describes a right adrenal tumor that appears to be a pheochromocytoma, a type of tumor originating from the adrenal gland. The tumor is characterized by variable size, abundant granular cytoplasm, atypical nuclei, nuclear pleomorphisms, hyperchromasia, and rare atypical mitoses. The presence of nuclear inclusions and intracytoplasmic hyaline globules is also noted. Fusiformis cells are present in the tumor. Hemorrhagic alterations are observed, but the tumor does not exceed the surrounding adrenal cortex. Vascular lymphatic invasion is present. The tumor is classified as a malignant pheochromocytoma based on a PASS score of 9. The lumbo-aortic lymph node is reported as normal.

The pathology report describes a tumor that is 7.4 cm in size and appears yellowish in color. The tumor is well-separated from the surrounding tissue. Under a microscope, the tumor is observed to have a mixture of zelibalien and trabecular architecture. The nuclei are enlarged, and the cytoplasm is weakly eosinophilic. Some areas of the tumor show pigmentation and bleeding. There are no signs of abnormal cell division, atypical mitotic figures, or areas of tissue death. The tumor has infiltrated the capsule without destroying it. Invasions into blood vessels are observed in both the central and peripheral parts of the tumor. The surrounding soft tissue does not show any signs of tumor invasion. Stain tests show strong staining for synaptophysin, mild staining for chromogranin, and weakly positive staining for sustentacular cells. The proliferation index (Ki67) is less than 5%. The final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma.

The pathology report describes a 4.2 cm nodule that is sharply demarcated from the surrounding tissues. Histologically, the tumor has a mixture of alveolar and trabecular patterns. It consists of large polygonal cells with round to ovoid nuclei. There is no increased mitotic activity or abnormal mitotic figures. No necrosis is present. The capsule of the tumor is infiltrated, but there is no destruction. The peri-adrenal adipose tissue is free of tumor, and there is no evidence of vascular invasion. The tumor cells are strongly positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin, while sustentacular cells at the periphery of the neoplastic cell clusters are positive for S100 protein. The proliferative fraction, as measured by Ki-67 staining, is less than 1%. The conclusion of the report is that it is a pheochromocytoma.

The pathology report is difficult to interpret due to the inclusion of incomplete and inconsistent information. It seems to be a report on a specimen from the left adrenal gland, which was received fresh in a medium container. The specimen showed a tumor with disrupted and previously incised areas, as well as pink-tan and hemorrhagic tissue. The tumor was encapsulated and measured 3.2 cm × 3.2 cm. The report mentions a frozen section control for tumor evaluation, but does not provide the results of that evaluation. The report also mentions additional tumor sections and a permanent section, but does not provide any details about these. Overall, the report lacks clear and concise information for a comprehensive summary.

The pathology report describes a gross examination of a tumor in the left adrenal gland. The tumor is ovoid in shape, measuring 90x60x45 mm and weighing 72 g. It has a fibrous capsule measuring 60x50x45 mm. On cut, the adrenal cortex appears yellow and measures 2 mm thick, while the tumor has a grey-pink color and soft consistency, with central hemorrhage.

Microscopically, the tumor is found to be a pheochromocytoma with diffuse alveolar growth. It has a fibrous capsule with signs of fresh and old hemorrhage and scarification. Remnants of the regular adrenal cortex are found at the periphery of the tumor. Immunohistochemistry shows no positive sustentacular cells and a positive internal control with small nerves in the periadrenal tissue.

Further examination reveals features that indicate the tumor's behavior and characteristics. It is classified as a WHO grade 2 pheochromocytoma with large nests or diffuse growth representing more than 10% of the tumor volume. There is central or confluent tumor necrosis, high cellularity, cellular monotony, and tumor cell spindling (even if focal). There are also more than 3 mitotic figures per 10 high-power fields, atypical mitotic figure(s), extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, capsular invasion, profound nuclear pleomorphism.

The report does not include the procurement date or confirmation date.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the left adrenal gland. The tumor is histologically characterized by an alveolar architecture composed of zellballen separated by thin layers of connective tissue. The tumor cells have a relatively broad eosinophil to basophil granular cytoplasm and large, pleomorphic nuclei with coarse chromatin. Some cells have very large, bizarre, and enlarged nuclei. There is evidence of a single atypical mitosis, but no necrosis, vessel invasion, capsule destruction, or invasion into adjacent adipose tissue. The PAS staining score is 3. The final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma with a PASS-Score of 3 out of a maximum of 20.

This pathology report describes the findings from the examination of a left adrenal mass that was suspected to be a pheochromocytoma. The tumor size is 3.0 x 2.5 x 2.0 cm. The histologic examination confirms the diagnosis of a pheochromocytoma. The tumor shows nested and diffuse architecture, with high cellularity, focal spindle cell cytology, marked nuclear pleomorphism, and focal nuclear hyperchromasia. There is no evidence of tumor necrosis, high mitotic activity, atypical mitotic figures, cellular monotony, extra-adrenal extension, or vascular invasion. The tumor extends to the inked surfaces and the cautery margin, indicating possible surgical margin involvement. The total score for tumor grading is 8 out of 20, suggesting potentially aggressive behavior. Further evaluation may be required to assess the metastatic potential of the tumor.

The pathology report describes a paraganglioma in the neck of a 49-year-old female. The tumor consists of monotonous cells with round nuclei, prominent red nucleoli, and eosinophilic cytoplasm. These cells are arranged in small nests surrounded by a delicate capillary network. There is a low mitotic activity (one mitotic figure per 10 high-power fields). Fibroelastic bands and entrapped nerve fibers are present, but there is no evidence of necrosis. The diagnosis is a neck tumor-paraganglioma.

The patient in question had a clinical diagnosis of pheochromocytoma and underwent a retroperitoneal laparoscopic adrenalectomy. The pathology report states that the right adrenal gland was resected and contained a 6.5 cm encapsulated nodule. The nodule had a red-brown cut surface with areas of yellow-tan and possible hemorrhage. The adjacent adrenal gland showed a thin yellow-orange cortex and a thin red-brown medulla. The diagnosis of pheochromocytoma was confirmed in the resected gland.

The pathology report indicates that the patient underwent a left adrenalectomy and was diagnosed with a pheochromocytoma. The tumor size was 22 x 2 x 2 cm, and it weighed 41 grams. The tumor was confined to the adrenal gland, and the resection margins were free of tumor. No lymph nodes were received with the specimen. Additional features of the tumor included absence of blood vessel invasion, absence of lymph vessel invasion, mitotic activity < 5/50 high power field, mild nuclear atypia, absence of necrosis, and low nuclear positivity on immunostain for MIB-1. The final stage of the tumor was pT1 with pNX lymph nodes and pMX distant metastasis. The gross description of the specimen indicates an enlarged adrenal gland with a well-encapsulated mass. The rest of the adrenal gland showed cortical hypertrophy.

This pathology report describes the findings of a lymph node next to a pheochromocytoma. The lymph node does not show any tumor localization. The pheochromocytoma itself is described as a cell-rich tumor with an alveolar pattern and epithelial cells. There are fibrous septa and small vessels between cell nests. The tumor cells have large cytoplasm, round nuclei with granular chromatin, and distinct nucleoli. There are scattered mitoses and brown to black pigment in the cells. Focal necrosis and hemorrhage are present, as well as expansive growth and capsular invasion. Fibrosis and sclerosis are seen in some areas. Thrombosis of vessels is present in many places. Electron microscopy supports the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma, as numerous secretory granules and mitochondria are seen in the tumor cells. Immunopathology shows positive results for certain markers. The final conclusion is an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma with necrotic areas and focal capsular invasion, with no vascular invasion or adrenal remnants identified.

This pathology report describes a surgical resection of a paraganglioma in a patient with a suspected pheochromocytoma. The final diagnosis confirms the presence of a celiac artery paraganglioma, with multifocal extension to the edges of the specimen. A lymph node from the celiac artery was also biopsied, but no tumor or lymph node was observed. The report mentions focal vascular and capsular invasion, diffuse growth, nuclear atypia, and high cellularity in the lesion. Immunohistochemical stains showed positive results for Chromogranin and synaptophysin, and a negative result for SDHB staining. Further molecular/genetic testing is recommended for possible SDHB germline mutation. The frozen section diagnosis was deferred to permanent analysis. The gross description provided details about the appearance and dimensions of the specimens received for analysis.

The pathology report describes an excised tumor that is diagnosed as an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, measuring 4.2 cm in its greatest dimension. There is a microscopic focus of invasion into adjacent fat, but no evidence of vascular invasion or necrosis. Mitoses are rare, and the Ki-67 labeling index is low. There are occasional small areas of neuron-like differentiation present. Immunohistochemical stains show varying numbers of sustentacular cells throughout the tumor. The report also mentions an intra-operative consultation with frozen section that confirms the diagnosis. The gross description describes the tumor as an encapsulated mass of dark red-purple and tan-red tissue, without evidence of capsular invasion. Additional studies have been performed using immunohistochemical staining.

This pathology report describes a surgical specimen labeled as the right adrenal gland, which was removed from a patient with a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. The adrenal gland weighs 109.5 grams and measures 2.5 x 4.0 x 5.4 cm. On sectioning, the tumor measures 2.5 x 2.5 x 3.0 cm. The tumor shows solid nesting architecture with polygonal cells having indistinct cell borders, abundant basophilic cytoplasm, and focal nuclear pleomorphism. There is evidence of vascular congestion and focal stromal hemorrhage, but no invasion or involvement of the surrounding tissue, lymph nodes, or resection margins. No other adrenal pathology is identified.

Summary: This pathology report is for a patient who underwent a right adrenal gland adrenalectomy. The diagnosis is pheochromocytoma, an uncommon type of tumor that arises from the adrenal medulla. The gross description of the specimen reveals a well-delineated mass with a bright yellow to yellow-orange cut surface. Microscopically, the tumor shows solid nesting and trabecular architecture with round cells that have clear to basophilic cytoplasm. There is no evidence of degeneration or invasion. The tumor is positive for chromogranin and tyrosine hydroxylase on immunohistochemistry. No other adrenal pathology or lymph node involvement is identified.

This pathology report summarizes the findings from the examination of a tumor specimen labeled as a para-aortic mass. The tumor is diagnosed as a paraganglioma, with indeterminate invasion given the incomplete evaluation of the tumor capsule. Margins are involved by the tumor, and lymph-vascular invasion and perineural invasion are not detected. No lymph node involvement or distant metastasis is identified. The tumor measures 2.4 cm in greatest dimension. The report also mentions difficulty in defining capsular lymphovascular invasion due to limited extratumoral material in the specimen. Immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests performed for diagnosis were developed by the laboratory and are certified for high complexity clinical laboratory testing.

This pathology report describes an adrenal gland specimen that was removed from a patient. The report states that a gallbladder was also listed on the requisition with this specimen, but it arrived in surgical pathology later with a liver biopsy from the same patient. The clinical information mentions that the patient had a history of gallstones and that the adrenal mass was found during examination related to the ordering protocol.

The gross description of the specimen reveals a soft tissue fragment labeled as "RIGHT ADRENAL." It measures 5.5 x 5.0 x 3.0 cm and weighs 48.5 grams. The specimen shows a soft, fleshy, tan tumor tissue with multiple areas of hemorrhage, measuring 5.0 cm in the largest dimension. A fragment of normal adrenal tissue is also attached to the tumor. The normal adrenal tissue shows a previous incision, but no tissue was collected from this site.

The report states that the specimen was inked blue, avoiding the previous incision and procurement site. Representative sections of the specimen were submitted in white cassettes, and the remainder of the specimen was returned to formalin for storage. It also mentions that the specimen was requested by a healthcare professional.

The pathology report describes an adrenal gland specimen that measures 10x6.5x7 cm. The specimen is encapsulated and shows a yellow lesion with brown inclusions, hemorrhage, and cystic transformation. Microscopically, normal adrenal tissue is observed, along with polygonal cells with fine granular inclusions and an eosinophilic cytoplasm. The nuclei of these cells are large and have prominent nucleoli with core inclusions. At the margins of the tumor, there is collagen-rich connective tissue and fatty tissue with infiltrates of pleomorphic cells. The atypical cells stain brown. The diagnosis is a 10cm pheochromocytoma.

The pathology report is for a patient who underwent a left adrenalectomy and was found to have a pheochromocytoma. Immunohistochemistry tests showed positive results for chromogranin, synaptophysin, and CD56 in the tumor cells. Gross examination of the specimen revealed a large left adrenal mass with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. The majority of the viable tumor was collected for further testing, along with a small portion of uninvolved adrenal tissue. The report notes that the laboratory is certified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing.

The pathology report describes the findings of an adrenal gland removal surgery. The final diagnosis is a pheochromocytoma (4 cm) with infarction and cystic degeneration. There is no evidence of capsular or vascular invasion, tumor necrosis is absent, and mitoses are extremely rare. Immunohistochemical stains show low labeling overall with scattered small hot spots. Sustentacular cells and focal neuronal differentiation are observed. The report also mentions that THC is positive for SOHB protein, suggesting that a mutation of SOHBx is not present. The gross description of the specimen indicates a hemorrhagic mass with a central cyst, partially encased by the adrenal capsule. The adjacent adrenal gland is grossly uninvolved.

The pathology report indicates that a 47-year-old patient underwent a laparoscopic adrenalectomy to remove a pheochromocytoma from the right adrenal gland. The tumor was well-circumscribed, measuring 3.5 x 3.5 cm, and originated from the medulla of the adrenal gland. The cortex of the gland appeared normal. The excised tumor measured 3.0 cm in its greatest dimension. The report confirms the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma.

This pathology report describes a tumor in the left adrenal gland. The tumor is soft with a diameter of 7.5 cm and has cystic lesions up to 3.7 cm in diameter. It is surrounded by a thin capsule. 

Histologically, the tumor is composed of Zellballen, which are clusters of cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. The cells have enlarged nuclei with prominent chromatin and sometimes macronucleoli. There are 2 mitoses per high-power field and no atypical mitosis. Some areas of bleeding and small necroses are present. There is no evidence of vessel invasion or capsule destruction.

Immunohistochemical staining shows positive results for synaptophysin, CD56, and chromogranin. S100 staining shows a reduced number of sustentacular cells. Negative staining is observed for AE 1/3, EMA, and p53. The Ki67 proliferation index is less than 1%.

The final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma.

The pathology report describes the examination of three specimens: a left adrenal mass, a retroperitoneal mass, and a second retroperitoneal mass. 

A. Left adrenal mass: 
- Diagnosis: Paraganglioma, extra-adrenal (located 0.3 cm from the left adrenal gland)
- Size: 3.5 cm
- The tumor infiltrates adjacent adipose tissue and extends to the resection surface
- No necrosis or significant histopathologic change in the adjacent adrenal gland

B. Retroperitoneal mass:
- Diagnosis: Benign ganglion, no neoplasm seen

C. Retroperitoneal mass #2:
- Diagnosis: Benign ganglion, no neoplasm seen

Additional information:
- The paraganglioma cells show positive staining for chromogranin and synaptophysin, and absence of staining for inhibin.
- The estimated proliferative fraction is low, with less than 5% in most areas.
- The patient is a male with an adrenal mass, suspected to be a pheochromocytoma.
- The left adrenal mass consists of an adrenal gland with an attached yellow lobulated fibrofatty tissue. A nodule within the mass is separate from the adrenal gland but located near it.
- Frozen section diagnosis during the surgery indicated an adrenal gland mass consistent with pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma and benign ganglion for the retroperitoneal masses.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the left adrenal gland that is 2.2 cm in diameter. The tumor is composed of zellballen and trabecular architecture. The cells are medium-sized with moderately pleomorphic features, enlarged nuclei with small nucleoli and amphophilic granular cytoplasm. The tumor is surrounded by a thin fibrous capsule that is invaded by the tumor in two locations, extending into the adjacent adipose tissue. There is a hematoma within the tumor, causing difficulty in complete resection. There is no evidence of necrosis, vessel invasion, increased mitosis, or atypical mitosis. The final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma CD-6-3.

This pathology report describes two specimens that were sent for analysis. The first specimen is soft tissue from the periaortic area, which shows fibroadipose tissue with cauterized cellular fragments. The second specimen is a left adrenal mass, which is diagnosed as a pheochromocytoma without any vascular or capsular invasion. The report mentions that further immunohistochemistry will be performed to characterize the cells in the soft tissue specimen. The report also includes information about the clinical history and procedure, as well as the gross description of the specimens received.

The pathology report describes a case involving a patient with a multinodular goiter and a fine needle aspiration revealing medullary thyroid carcinoma. A CT scan showed the presence of a right adrenal tumor which was subsequently removed through right adrenalectomy. The right adrenal gland measured 8.68 grams and contained a 1.6 x 1.5 x 1.3 cm brown circumscribed mass surrounded by yellow cortical tissue. Tissue procurement was performed on central portions of the tumor, and the remaining nodule and adjacent gland were submitted for further examination. The final diagnosis was pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland.

Summary: The pathology report confirms the diagnosis of a pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland. The tumor mass measured 3.3 cm and appeared well-encapsulated. The remaining adrenal tissue was noted at the edge of the specimen. No cystic spaces were identified. The report does not provide further details or information about the patient.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the right adrenal gland. The tumor weighs 48 g and measures 69x50x30 mm. It is an ovoid encapsulated grey-pink tumor with a soft consistency. The tumor is a pheochromocytoma with focal fibrotization and multiple cellular atypias. It has a fibrous capsule, and remnants of the adrenocortical structures are found on the periphery. There is evidence of penetration through adrenocortical structures and initial invasion through the fibrous adrenal capsule in one of the blocks examined. No spread into the surrounding adipose tissue was found. Staining for $100 protein was positive in some parts of the tumor but rare or vanished in less differentiated parts. MIBI staining was less than 1%, which was the positive control. Based on the findings, the tumor meets several criteria for malignancy, including large nests or diffuse growth, tumor necrosis, high cellularity, cellular monotony, spindling of tumor cells, mitotic figures, atypical mitotic figures, extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, and nuclear hyperchromasia. The total score for these criteria is 7. The report does not state the dates of the procurement or confirmation of the tumor.

The pathology report indicates that the specimen received for examination was labeled as the right adrenal gland. The diagnosis made is a pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal gland. There is no evidence of invasion into surrounding tissues, tumor cell death, or abnormal mitosis. The gross examination describes the size and appearance of the adrenal gland and the microscopic examination confirms the presence of a pheochromocytoma. No administrative notes or charges are associated with this case.

Summary of Pathology Report:

The report describes a tumor in the left adrenal gland measuring 3.5x3.2x3 cm. The tumor is characterized by neoplastic growth in the adrenal medulla, causing partial compression of the adrenal cortex. The tumor cells have oval-shaped nuclei, peripheral nucleoli, and large amounts of chromatin. The mitotic rate is low at 2 per 10 high-power fields. There is no evidence of vascular invasion or necrosis. The tumor expresses inhibin alpha and S-100. The final diagnosis is a pheochromocytoma of the left adrenal gland.

The pathology report describes a surgical specimen from the left adrenal gland, which measures 9.5x8x5.5 cm and contains a tumor mass measuring 4.5x3.5x9 cm. The tumor appears multi-nodular with necrosis in the center. Microscopically, it is identified as a malignant pheochromocytoma. The report confirms the presence of malignant features, including large areas of proliferative growth, central necrosis, and cellular atypia. The diagnosis of malignant pheochromocytoma is supported by these findings. There is no evidence of disease in two small lymph nodes examined.

The pathology report describes a left adrenal tumor, weighing 60g and measuring 80x50x35 mm. The tumor consists of two adjacent nodules, with the smaller one measuring 25x35x20 mm and the larger one measuring 60x40x40 mm. On examination, both nodules appear grey-pink and soft, with a yellow scarification in the center of the larger nodule. Microscopically, both nodules are found to be pheochromocytomas with large regressive changes in the center of the larger nodule. There are remnants of adrenal cortex with pressure atrophy and some extracapsular proliferates on the periphery of the tumor. The excisions do not show infiltration of the periadrenal tissue by pheochromocytoma. Immunohistochemical examination reveals the presence of sustentacular cells and a low proliferation index (MIB-1 < 1%). The tumor does not meet the criteria for large nests or diffuse growth, central or confluent tumor necrosis, high cellularity, cellular monotony, tumor cell spindling, vascular invasion, capsular invasion, profound nuclear pleomorphism, nuclear hyperchromasia, or high mitotic activity. The report does not include information about the procurement date or confirmation date.

The pathology report indicates the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland. The specimen taken for analysis was a right adrenalectomy measuring 7.5 x 5 x 2 cm and weighing 44.6 grams. The specimen had a soft texture and a red-tan semiliquid center. A small portion of normal adrenal tissue was found at the superior pole of the tumor. No lymph node or secondary mass was noted in the periadrenal fat. Vascular invasion is mentioned as a risk factor for malignancy.

This pathology report describes the findings from a surgical procedure involving the removal of the right adrenal gland (adrenalectomy) and the spleen (splenectomy). 

The diagnosis for the adrenal gland is Pheochromocytoma, which is a tumor found in the adrenal gland that produces excessive amounts of adrenaline and noradrenaline. 

The diagnosis for the spleen is Sarcoidosis, a condition characterized by the growth of tiny collections of inflammatory cells (granulomas) in various parts of the body. No tumor or evidence of metastatic pheochromocytoma was found in the spleen.

Additional tests were performed to rule out fungal organisms or mycobacteria, but none were found. Further clinical correlation is recommended to determine the cause of the spleen findings.

Immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests were performed for diagnosis, but they have not been cleared or approved by the FDA.

The gross description indicates the size and appearance of the specimens received for analysis. 

Overall, the pathology report confirms the diagnoses of a pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland and sarcoidosis in the spleen.

This pathology report describes a case of a para-aortic neuroendocrine tumor. A mass was removed from the patient's anterior to the descending aorta during surgery. The specimen was labeled as a "paraaortic ganglioma" and measured 6.0x3.5 x 3.0m. The initial diagnosis from the operating room was fibroadipose tissue and vessel, no tumor seen. Additional sections were submitted for further analysis. The final report describes the specimen as a yellow-tan soft tissue fragment with a homogeneous fleshy pink-tan cut surface. Further analysis was performed on the specimen and sections were submitted for examination. No consultants were involved in the case. The report is signed and dated by the resident who performed the analysis.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the right adrenal gland. The tumor is red to brown in color and measures 5.5 cm in diameter. Microscopically, the tumor is surrounded by a fibrous capsule and consists of Zellballen, which are clusters of cells with a trabecular architecture. The nuclei of the cells are round to oval with smooth chromatin. Dilated blood vessels can be seen in the septal areas surrounding the Zellballen, and there is evidence of single areas of necrosis in the center of the tumor. There is no significant increase in the number of mitoses, no profound nuclear pleomorphism, vessel invasion, or capsule destruction. The final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma.

The pathology report describes the findings of a left and right adrenalectomy. The patient's clinical history includes recently revealed hypertension and investigations revealed bilateral adrenal nodules attributed to pheochromocytoma. 

Macroscopy: The left adrenal specimen weighs 14g and measures 6.5 x 2.5 x 2.5 cm. After cutting, a grayish nodule measuring 1 cm is observed. The right adrenal specimen weighs 23g and measures 6.5 x 4 x 4 cm, with a grayish beige tumor measuring 2 cm.

Microscopy: In the left adrenal, there is a proliferation of tumor cells organized into bays or small nests within a vascularized tissue. The tumor cells are large with polygonal basophilic cytoplasm. The nuclei exhibit slight anisokaryosis with a small visible nucleolus. There is no mitosis or necrosis. The tumor is limited by a fibrous condensation separating it from the rest of the adrenal tissue. No capsular infiltration or tumor embolus is seen. The outside of the adrenal is normal. The PASS score is 0, indicating no features suggestive of malignancy.

IHC study shows that the tumor cells express chromogranin, synaptophysin, and N Cam.

Conclusion: Left adrenal - Benign pheochromocytoma measuring 1 cm. PASS Score = 0. Right adrenal - Benign pheochromocytoma measuring 2 cm. PASS Score = 0. The cytological and immunchistochemical characteristics are identical to those described.

The pathology report describes a case of a 42-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and two left adrenal masses. The patient underwent a laparoscopic left adrenalectomy for a pheochromocytoma. 

The final diagnosis reveals that the left adrenal gland weighed 41.2g and contained two distinct masses. One mass, measuring 2.2 cm, was identified as a pheochromocytoma and was completely excised. The other mass, measuring 2.0 cm, was diagnosed as an adrenal cortical adenoma and was also completely excised. The report also mentions the presence of focal necrosis, high cellularity, tumor cell spindling, mitoses, nuclear pleomorphism, and nuclear hyperchromasia in the pheochromocytoma lesion. 

Immunohistochemical stains were performed, revealing positive staining for synaptophysin, chromogranin, and S100 in the pheochromocytoma cells. The K-67 staining indicated a low proliferation index. Additionally, immunostaining for SDHB was conducted, showing moderate cytoplasmic staining in the tumor cells. 

The report includes a disclaimer regarding the use of certain reagents for in-vitro immunohistochemical tests, stating that they have not been cleared or approved by the FDA but have been validated for diagnostic use. The report also provides a gross description of the specimen, noting the sizes and characteristics of the masses. No other masses or lesions were identified.

This pathology report describes the findings from an adrenalectomy on both the right and left adrenal glands. Both glands showed the presence of pheochromocytoma, which is a tumor of the adrenal gland. Immunohistochemistry tests were performed and showed positive staining for NSE, Synaptophysin, Chromogranin, and CD56 in the tumor cells. The tumor cells also stained negative for inhibin. The report notes that the laboratory performing the tests is certified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing and that the tests performed have not been cleared or approved by the FDA. The report includes a detailed description of the size and appearance of the tumor masses and normal tissue in both adrenal glands. No additional consultants were involved in the analysis.

Summary:
The pathology report describes a tumor in the left adrenal gland, weighing 219g and measuring 120x80x55 mm. The tumor is encapsulated and shows large areas of necrosis. There is a presence of cellulization, granular neutrophils, siderophagic cleaning reaction, and beginning fibrotization at the border of the necrotic areas. Immunohistochemical examination showed strong positive staining for chromogranin and negative staining for adrenal cortex and periadrenal adipose tissue. The MIB1 index was 3-5%. No angioinvasion or capsular invasion was found, but there was extension into adipose tissue. The tumor also showed features such as large nests or diffuse growth, tumor cell spindling, high cellularity, and mitotic figures. The final PASS score was 8. The procurement and confirmation dates were not provided in the summary.

This pathology report is for a patient who underwent an exploratory laparotomy, resection of a periaortic mass, pen cholecystectomy, and open paroesophageal hernia repair. The report indicates the findings of the following specimens:  

1. Retroperitoneal mass: A lobular, well-encapsulated mass measuring 6.8 x 5.9 x 4.5 cm. The cut surfaces show scattered calcifications, hemorrhage, and central areas of fibrosis. No necrotic areas are observed. The mass is encapsulated within a thick fibrotic sheath.

2. Right portal lymph node: A lymph node measuring 1.12 x 0.9 x 0.6 cm with attached adipose tissue. It appears to be a benign lymph node with no evidence of neoplasm.

3. Gallbladder: The gallbladder measures 7.64 x 6.5 x 1.4 cm. The serosal surfaces have a 0.6 cm transmural defect in the fundus. The mucosa appears diffusely green-yellow and trabeculated. The wall is diffusely thickened up to 0.8 cm, and the lumen contains green, viscous bile. No calculi or other abnormalities are identified.

The report is signed by the pathologist who personally examined and interpreted the slides from this case.

The pathology report confirms the final diagnosis of a left adrenal gland resection showing a pheochromocytoma. The tumor is surrounded by a fibrous capsule and appears to be completely excised with no evidence of tumor protruding into blood vessels or thrombus. The report does not provide any information about the pre-operative or post-operative diagnosis. The gross description describes the appearance of the specimen, including its size, color, and capsule thickness. Representative sections of the tissue are submitted for further study.

The pathology report indicates that the patient had a left adrenalectomy and possible left nephrectomy, distal pancreatectomy, and splenectomy. The report describes the specimen received, which includes a 6.9 cm and a 3.0 cm mass with different morphologies, both identified as pheochromocytoma. The report suggests a syndrome form is likely given the patient's young age and recent diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma. No lymphovascular invasion is identified. Additionally, a fragment of soft tissue adjacent to the aorta is excised, with no tumor identified. The report concludes that two discrete tumors are favored.

The pathology report describes a left adrenal pheochromocytoma, which is a tumor of the adrenal gland. The tumor measures 9 cm and has a solid cystic hemorrhagic appearance. The tumor cells are large and eosinophilic with abundant cytoplasm and occasional hyaline globules. The nuclei show some degree of anisokaryosis (variation in size), pale chromatin, and prominent nucleoli. The tumor is highly cellular and shows some cellular monotony. Mitoses (cell division) are rare, with only one observed in 10 fields of view. There is no atypical mitosis. The tumor is often highly hemorrhagic with fibrous and cystic reorganizations, and there is abundant hemosiderin deposition. There is no evidence of capsular invasion or vascular invasion, and there is no necrosis. The report gives a PASS score of 6, indicating diffuse architecture, high cellularity, and cellular monotony. Overall, the report confirms the presence of a 9 cm left adrenal pheochromocytoma.

Summary: The pathology report describes a tumor in the left adrenal gland measuring 5x4.1x4 cm. The tumor is tan in color and is surrounded by a thin layer of normal adrenal tissue. Histologically, the tumor consists of zellballen (a characteristic pattern of cells seen in certain tumors) surrounded by connective tissue. The tumor cells are enlarged but do not show signs of mitosis or necrosis. There are focal destructions of the capsula, indicating invasion into adjacent adipose tissue. Immunohistochemical staining shows strong positivity for synaptophysin and chromogranin, indicating neuroendocrine differentiation. MART1 stains positive only in the adjacent adrenal parenchyma, while inhibin stains strongly positive in the normal adrenal tissue but weakly positive in the tumor. Additionally, the Ki67 proliferation index is less than 1%. Based on these findings, the final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma.

The pathology report is summarizing findings from a tumor in the adrenal gland. The tumor measures 4 x 2.7 x 2 cm and is encapsulated. There is a second smaller fragment measuring 4 x 1 x 0.5 cm. The tumor contains polygonal cells with abundant cytoplasm and nucleolated nuclei. There is a honeycomb structure and a large vascular network within the tumor. Sustentacular cells with basophilic nuclei are also present. There is no evidence of vascular or capsule invasion, and rare mitotic figures are seen. There is no tumor necrosis. The surrounding fat tissue consists of mature adipatic cells. The conclusion is that this is a benign pheochromocytoma with a PASS score of 0.

The pathology report indicates that the following specimens were submitted: a paracaval lymph node and a right retroperitoneal mass. The report confirms the presence of a paraganglioma (extraadrenal pheochromocytoma) in the right retroperitoneal mass. No tumor was seen in the lymph nodes. The report also notes that immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests were performed for diagnosis. The report states that the laboratory is certified and qualified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing.

The pathology report describes two findings: 
1. Adrenal gland, right, adrenalectomy: The presence of a pheochromocytoma (a tumor of the adrenal gland) measuring 3.4 cm in greatest dimension.
2. Skin, right lower back lesion, biopsy: The presence of a neurofibroma (a benign tumor of the nerves) in a circular soft tissue fragment measuring 1.2 cm in diameter.
