The tumor is composed of nests of neuroendocrine cells and sustentacular cells, as confirmed by immunostaining. Inhibin is negative.

The pathology report describes a surgical specimen that weighs 75g and measures 7.5x6x3.5 cm. It contains a mass that measures 50x50x35mm. An adrenal gland is present at the periphery of the specimen.

The microscopic examination of the tumor reveals tumoral cells with big size, clear cytoplasm, nuclei with thickened chromatin, clear nucleolus, and clear and abundant cytoplasm. The tumor has moderate nuclear atypia and 5 mitoses per 50 high-power fields (HPF). The architecture of the tumor is trabecular with a vascular stroma. There is no necrosis observed. At the periphery, the tumor is surrounded by a fibrous pseudo-capsule and infiltrates the adipose tissue. Some nervous fibers are found within the tumor but there is no real invasion. Vascular invasion is not present. 

The lymph node of the hepatic pedicle is negative for tumor involvement. The gallbladder is found to be normal. 

The conclusion of the report is that the patient has a malignant pheochromocytoma measuring 50x50x30mm. There is no vascular invasion. The lymph node of the hepatic pedicle is negative for tumor involvement and the gallbladder is normal.

The pathology report describes the findings from a surgical resection of a pheochromocytoma in the left adrenal gland. The tumor is encapsulated and measures 10.9 x 6.8 x 14.2 cm. It shows lobular architecture and is located adjacent to the seminal vessels and adipose tissue of the renal hilum. The kidney itself appears normal, with no invasion by the tumor. Several lymph nodes initially suspected to be involved are found to be directly connected to the main mass of the tumor, indicating metastasis. The lymph nodes are serially sectioned and show areas of hemorrhage. The tumor is found to involve both perinephric and renal hilar adipose tissue and shows vascular invasion. The surgical margins are negative for tumor involvement. Two periaortic lymph nodes are excised and confirmed to be metastatic pheochromocytoma. Overall, the left kidney and adrenal gland are removed, and two lymph nodes are found to have metastatic pheochromocytoma.

This pathology report describes the findings of a specimen labeled "right adrenal" and "gallbladder." 

For the right adrenal specimen, the diagnosis is a pheochromocytoma, which is a tumor of the adrenal gland. The tumor is well-circumscribed and encapsulated, and there is no evidence of infiltration into surrounding structures. There are no signs of increased mitotic activity or tumor necrosis, except for one focus of vascular invasion. The report recommends clinical follow-up as histologic features may not always correlate with the tumor's behavior.

For the gallbladder specimen, the diagnosis is chronic cholecystitis with cholesterolosis. The gallbladder is intact, with no stones present. The mucosa is dark brown with diffuse yellow speckling.

Only representative sections of both specimens were submitted for further examination.

The pathology report describes a 42 g tumor specimen that is reddish to light-colored, measuring 5x4x3 cm. The tumor is composed of medium-sized cells with enlarged nuclei, well distinguishable nucleoli, and some pleomorph nuclei. There is one area of sclerosis with necrosis, but no extensive necrosis or increased number of mitosis. There is no evidence of vessel invasion. The final diagnosis is an extra-adrenal paraganglioma.

This pathology report is for a patient who underwent a right adrenalectomy to remove a tumor. The final diagnosis of the tumor is a pheochromocytoma. The size of the tumor is 4x1.8x1.5 cm and it weighs 21 grams. The tumor is confined to the adrenal gland with minimal capsular invasion. The margins of resection are free of tumor and there is no blood or lymph vessel invasion. The tumor shows a diffuse pattern of growth with high cellularity and cellular monotony. Mitotic activity is high, with 15-18 mitoses per 20 high power field, and there is moderate nuclear atypia. Necrosis is absent. Ancillary studies including immunohistochemistry reveal moderately positive staining for synaptophysin and strongly positive staining for chromogranin. The tumor is negative for EMA. The pTN stage is pT1, and regional lymph node involvement and distant metastasis cannot be assessed. The intra-operative consultation with frozen section confirms neoplasia in the right adrenal gland. The pre-operative diagnosis and gross description are not provided in the report.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the right adrenal gland that has been identified as a pheochromocytoma. Immunohistochemical staining showed positive staining for synaptophysin and chromogranin, and negative staining for inhibin, SF1, Calretinin, MART1, and KL1. Only a small number of cells stained positive for Ki67, indicating a low rate of proliferation. The total score for the tumor was 3, indicating a benign disease.

The pathology report describes the findings from an adrenalectomy performed on the right adrenal gland. Fragments of a pheochromocytoma tumor were identified. The tumor shows areas of hemorrhage and has focal tumor cell spindling and marked nuclear pleomorphism. However, necrosis, capsular invasion, vascular invasion, and extension into peri-adrenal adipose tissue are not present. Mitotic figures are also relatively low. The report mentions that the Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score (PASS) for this tumor is less than 4, indicating that it is expected to behave in a benign manner. The report also notes that tumors with a PASS score of 4 or higher have the potential for more aggressive behavior. Representative tissue sections have been submitted for further analysis.

The pathology report is for a surgical specimen of a right adrenal mass that was found to be a pheochromocytoma with areas suggestive of diverged differentiation. Immunohistochemistry studies were performed and were positive for Chromogranin, Synaptophysin, and S-100, and negative for C-Kit and NFTP. The specimen consists of a tumor mass with an additional rim of tissue resembling normal adrenal. The tumor has a variegated brown, tan, and yellow cut surface with an area of deep red. Small sections of normal-appearing adrenal tissue and representative sections of the tumor are submitted for permanent processing. There are no consultants involved in the case.

The pathology report indicates the following findings:

1. Pheochromocytoma: Adrenal (left) adrenalectomy specimen.
2. Extra-adrenal paraganglioma: Ganglia, 1 of 3 (para-aortic suprahilar) biopsies.
3. No pathological diagnosis: Gallbladder.
4. No pathological diagnosis: Lymph node, 1 (supra-pancreatic) biopsy.
5, 6, 7. inftrating neuroendocrine carcinoma: Soft tissue (#6 site not specified, portal vein and retroperitoneum) biopsies.

11. No pathological diagnosis: Duodenum.

The synoptic data provides additional information about the tumor and its characteristics. The tumor is a pancreatic endocrine tumor located in the head of the pancreas. It is unifocal and infiltrative, with a size of 5.0 cm. No regional lymph node metastasis is found. Invasion of other margins (specimens 5, 6, and 7) is observed. No venous/lymphatic invasion or perineural invasion is present. Mitotic activity is absent. Immunohistochemistry shows positive staining for synaptophysin and chromogranin, and focal staining for insulin. Other staining markers are negative.

The clinical history states that the tumor is located in the pancreas. The gross description provides details about the size and appearance of the specimens received, including the adrenal gland and lymph nodes.

The pathology report indicates that the patient had a left adrenal gland removed through laparoscopic adrenalectomy. The diagnosis is pheochromocytoma, weighing 109 grams. The surgical margins were free of pheochromocytoma, and there was no lymphovascular space invasion identified. The tumor was circumscribed and encapsulated. No residual adrenal gland or cortex was seen in the specimen. Representative sections were taken for further analysis.

The pathology report is for an adrenalectomy (removal of the adrenal gland) performed on a woman with a left adrenal pheochromocytoma (a tumor that produces excess adrenaline) and an adrenal cortical adenoma (a benign tumor of the adrenal cortex).

The specimen submitted is the left adrenal gland, which is described as a 4x7.5x5.4 cm, red-yellow, cystic, lobulated mass. There is a dark red-yellow, cystic, lobulated cut surface, and a separate aggregate of tissue measuring 2.5x2.0x0.3 cm that is not involving the inked margin.

Representative sections of the adrenal cortex are submitted for further analysis.

The pathology report describes an adrenal tumor that was removed during a laparoscopic adrenalectomy. The tumor consisted of two nodules, one measuring 6.2 cm and the other measuring 3.1 cm. Both tumors appeared to be encapsulated and surrounded by a fine membrane. The larger tumor had a bright red, lobulated appearance with areas of fresh bleeding and focal necrosis, while the smaller tumor had a bright red-yellow appearance without necrosis. There was also intact adrenal cortex present. 

Microscopic examination of the tumors showed polymorphic cells arranged in nests and strands separated by vascular structures. The cells exhibited varying degrees of eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions. No significant necrosis or remarkable mitotic activity was observed. Immunohistochemistry staining indicated weak expression for chromogranin and S-100, and strong positivity for inhibin in the remaining adrenal cortex. The staining for ACTH was negative, ruling out ectopic ACTH production related to Cushing syndrome.

The overall interpretation of the pathology report is that the tumor is consistent with a pheochromocytoma. The surgical margins were free from tumor involvement.

This pathology report is for a surgical procedure involving the removal of a left adrenal mass (pheochromocytoma). The report confirms the presence of the tumor, which was not visible on the surface of the specimen. Immunohistochemical staining revealed patchy ganglion cells, and areas of micronodular hyperplasia were observed in the cortex. The diagnosis of pheochromocytoma was concurred by 10 individuals who reviewed the case. The gross description of the specimen indicates a tan/brown soft tissue mass measuring 8 x 5 x 4.5 cm and weighing 108 grams. The largest nodule within the mass measures 4.0 cm in diameter. No clearly demarcated normal adrenal gland was identified. A central piece from the largest nodule was procured for further examination. The specimen is consistent with the description and representative sections have been submitted for processing.

This pathology report describes the findings of a surgical pathologic examination of a specimen labeled "right adrenal." The specimen is a 97 gram, 9.5 x 8.0 x 4.0 cm portion of yellow-tan adipose tissue containing an intact adrenal gland. Serial sectioning of the specimen revealed a 6.0 x 5.3 x 4.3 cm soft, mottled, red-purple to brown mass within the adrenal medulla. The adrenal gland exhibits a bright orange cortex. Microscopic examination confirms the diagnosis of a pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland, with the presence of microscopic foci of vascular invasion. The biologic behavior of pheochromocytoma can be difficult to predict from the histology, but the presence of vascular invasion is a worrisome finding. Close clinical follow-up is recommended. A portion of fresh tissue was saved for tissue banking, and representative sections were submitted for further analysis.

The pathology report describes a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland. The margins of the tumor appear free of cancer cells. The specimen received is a fresh adrenal mass measuring 18.5x5x0 cm, with a nodule within the tissue measuring 3 cm. The tumor has a hemorrhagic appearance. A small portion of normal adrenal tissue is also present. The remaining tumor is submitted for further analysis.

The pathology report for case number 75664541-4362 reveals the following findings:

1. Right portal lymph node, frozen section: No tumor seen.
2. Tumor, right retroperitoneal, resection: Paraganglioma (Extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma).

The report also mentions that immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests were performed and developed by the Laboratory of Pathology, but they have not been cleared or approved by the FDA. The laboratory is certified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing.

The clinical history of the patient includes palpitations, tremors, and the presence of a retroperitoneal mass. The procedure identified a lobulated, circumscribed retroperitoneal mass. Specimens submitted for analysis include a right portal lymph node and the tumor.

The intraoperative consultation reported that the right portal lymph node showed no tumor. The gross description confirms the presence of a right retroperitoneal tumor, measuring approximately 3.8 cm x 2.5 cm x 3.8 cm, with variegated cut surfaces showing hemorrhagic areas and nodular yellow tissue.

The report concludes that the right retroperitoneal tumor is diagnosed as a paraganglioma, which is an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma. No consultants were involved in the analysis. The report is signed and dated by the responsible resident and sign out doctor.

The pathology report indicates that the specimen is from the right adrenal gland and weighs 102 grams. The adrenal gland measures 7.5 x 6.5 x 4.5 cm and contains a 5.3 cm encapsulated tumor. The tumor consists of trabecular and alveolar cells with small oval nuclei and eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm. Some areas of the tumor have enlarged, polymorphic nuclei with large nucleoli. There are no mitotic figures present. The tumor is surrounded by normal adrenocortical tissue and has a wide capsule. There is focal growth into the capsule but no invasion into blood vessels or surrounding adipose tissue. No hyperplasia of the normal adrenal tissue is observed, but there is dilation of blood vessels. Immunohistochemistry shows scattered positive staining for chromogranin and sporadic positive staining for S100. The conclusion is that the resected adrenal gland has a 5.3 cm pheochromocytoma with clear surgical margins.

The pathology report describes two specimens labeled as "Pheochromocytoma" and "Paraganglioma with focal extension into adipose tissue." The report states that the tumor measures 2.5 cm in size and is associated with sympathetic ganglia. It also mentions that the Ki-67 labeling index is moderately increased in the tumor cells. One lymph node tested negative for tumor cells. Additionally, a reactive lymph node with lipogranulomas was found. The report includes findings from intra-operative consultations with frozen sections, which were consistent with paraganglioma associated with sympathetic ganglion and reactive lymph node. The clinical history and pre- and post-operative diagnoses are not provided. The gloss descriptions provide details about the size, appearance, and slicing of the specimens.

This pathology report describes the findings of a robotic laparoscopic adrenalectomy on a 6-year-old female patient with a diagnosis of a left adrenal pheochromocytoma. The tumor measured 3.4 cm and weighed an estimated 18 g. The surgical margins were not involved by the tumor, and the adrenal gland away from the tumor appeared unremarkable. No lymph nodes were involved or examined. Immunohistochemical staining for Ki-67 showed a labeling index of <13. The specimen was received disrupted, making it difficult to measure the precise tumor mass, but it was estimated to be approximately 7 g. The patient's clinical history revealed an adrenal mass and elevated urine and serum metanephrines, consistent with pheochromocytoma. The gross description of the specimen indicated a well-circumscribed and necrotic tumor confined to the adrenal medulla. The tumor weighed 14.6 g and represented approximately 50% of the mass of the tissue. The tumor was 3.4 cm in size. The closest surgical margins were 1 mm to the non-disrupted side and less than 1 mm to the disrupted side. The adrenal gland away from the tumor appeared normal. No lymph nodes were identified. The tumor was submitted for further investigation.

This pathology report describes the findings of an adrenalectomy procedure on the right adrenal gland. The final diagnosis is a pheochromocytoma, with the tumor measuring 3x2.8x26 cm. The weight of the adrenal gland is 29 grams. The tumor is confined to the adrenal gland and the resection margins are free of tumor. No lymph node involvement is detected. The tumor shows marked nuclear atypia but no necrosis. Ancillary studies, including immunohistochemical studies, reveal certain characteristics of the tumor. The report also notes that there is no evidence of adrenal medullary hyperplasia or features associated with ven HippebLindau disease. The gross description provides additional details about the appearance of the specimen. The report is electronically signed by the pathologist who conducted the examination. The pre-operative and post-operative diagnoses are not provided.

The summary of the pathology report is as follows:

- A 58.8 gram mass was removed from the patient's right adrenal gland through a procedure called adrenalectomy.
- The mass is diagnosed as an adrenal pheochromocytoma measuring 12.9 cm in size, which was confined to the adrenal gland.
- The mass showed diffuse growth and invasion of the capsule and blood vessels.
- Immunohistochemical staining was performed to confirm the diagnosis, showing strong and diffuse positive reactions for chromogranin and negative staining for inhibin and SDHB.
- Gross examination of the specimen revealed an orange, smooth mass with occasional fluid-filled cysts and a solid nodule.
- Representative sections of the mass were submitted for further microscopic examination.
- The report includes a disclaimer stating that some tests were performed using reagents not cleared or approved by the FDA, but were validated for diagnostic use by the laboratory. These tests provide adjunctive information to assist with the morphologic evaluation.

The pathology report describes a left adrenal pheochromocytoma, a tumor in the adrenal gland, measuring 3 cm in length. The tumor is well-defined and has a trabecular or nest-like architecture. The cells of the tumor are densely packed and have basophilic cytoplasm. The nuclei of the cells are medium-sized, round, and non-hyperchromatic. There is no evidence of mitotic figures or infiltration into surrounding tissues. Immunohistochemical studies show that the tumor cells are positive for chromogranin, and the sustentacular network is preserved. The overall conclusion is a left adrenal pheochromocytoma with a PASS score of 4, indicating high cellularity and cellular monotony.

This pathology report describes the excision of the left and right adrenal glands, weighing 18.5g and 29.99g respectively, in a patient with von Hippel-Lindau disease and bilateral pheochromocytoma. The left adrenal gland contains a pheochromocytoma measuring 1.8cm and the right adrenal gland contains a pheochromocytoma measuring 6.0cm. Surrounding brown fat is also present in both glands. The report notes abnormal mitoses and marked nuclear pleomorphism in both lesions, with a PAS score of 5 for the left adrenal gland and 3 for the right adrenal gland. Gross descriptions and serial sectioning of the specimens are provided. Specimen 1 is submitted in 1A and 1B through 14 sections, while specimen 2 is submitted in 2A through 2M sections.

This is a pathology report for a patient who underwent a right adrenalectomy. The diagnosis is pheochromocytoma, with no evidence of vascular or capsular penetration identified. There are multiple small tumor fragments on the surface of the periadrenal fat, which are likely related to specimen handling and do not represent extracapsular invasion. Immunohistochemical staining showed positive results for chromogranin and synaptophysin, as well as sustentacular cells. The report also mentions that the immunoperoxidase tests performed have not been cleared or approved by the FDA but the laboratory is certified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing. The gross description of the specimen is provided, including its size and weight, as well as the presence of a mass with central necrosis. Representative sections of the tumor and normal adrenal gland were submitted for permanent processing.

The pathology report describes a 4.2x3.2x0.4cm tan tumor in the right adrenal gland with central necrosis and close proximity to the resection border. The tumor appears to be a pheochromocytoma, which is confirmed by immunohistochemical staining that showed positive staining for synaptophysin, weak staining for chromogranin, and identification of rare sustentacular cells. The tumor has a low proliferation index. The final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma.

This pathology report describes a surgical excision of a right adrenal mass, which was later diagnosed as a pheochromocytoma. The specimen received measured 5.3 grams and was labeled "Right Adrenal - Pheochromocytoma." The gross description indicates that the specimen was procured for the protocol and the remaining portion was submitted for routine processing. The specimen is inked black and representative sections are submitted for permanent assessment. Chromogranin staining was positive, confirming the diagnosis, and S-100 staining showed sustentacular cells.

The pathology report describes the findings from a surgical specimen of the left adrenal gland and a periaortic lymph node. The left adrenal gland contained a tumor called a pheochromocytoma, measuring 5.5 x 5 x 2.5 cm. The tumor showed focal invasion of the capsule and extension into the surrounding adipose tissue. However, there was no evidence of vascular invasion, necrosis, mitoses, nuclear pleomorphism, high cellularity, cellular monotony, or tumor cell spindling. The lymph node was negative for tumor cells. The report notes that while the tumor showed histomorphological features consistent with a pheochromocytoma with benign clinical behavior, further clinical and radiologic evaluation is needed to definitively determine its clinical behavior and rule out metastasis.

The pathology report indicates the following findings:

1. Adrenal gland, right, adrenalectomy: Consistent with pheochromocytoma.
2. Gallbladder, cholecystectomy: Gallbladder with cholelithiasis and mild chronic inflammation.

The report also mentions that immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests were performed for diagnosis, but they have not been cleared or approved by the FDA. The laboratory where the tests were conducted is certified under the CLIA to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing.

The clinical information states that the patient presented with Pheochromocytoma and Biliary Colic.

The gross descriptions of the specimens indicate the size, appearance, and notable features of the right adrenal gland and gallbladder that were removed. Sample sections were submitted for further analysis, and the remaining tissue was placed in formalin for further processing. The report also includes information about the requested by and date of signing the final report.

- This pathology report describes the findings from several specimens labeled A, B, F, C, and O.
- Specimens A and B are identified as adrenal mass and retroperitoneal lymph node, respectively. The adrenal mass measures 4.4 cm in its greatest dimension, while the lymph node measures 0.8 cm. Both specimens are entirely encapsulated and show no vascular invasion or tumor necrosis. The tumor cells stain positively for chromogranin, synaptophysin, and NSE, and are negative for EMA and ACTH. The sustentacular cells are positive for S-100. The proliferative index, as determined by the MIB-1 (Ki 67) immunostain, is less than 1%.
- Specimen F is a Whipple's resection, which reveals two duodenal carcinoids measuring 1.1 cm and 2 cm in their greatest dimension. The tumors have infiltrated into the muscularis propria and show psammomatous calcification in one case. Nodal metastasis is present in 2 out of 5 peripancreatic nodes, with focal extranodal extension. The tumor cells stain positively for chromogranin, synaptophysin, somatostatin, and S-100, as well as gastrin and CK7. However, stains for glucagon, insulin, pancreatic polypeptide, serotonin, ACTH, and CK20 are negative. The proximal and distal resection margins and the pancreas are free of tumor. The bile duct resection margin shows prominent acute inflammation with reactive atypia, but no evidence of malignancy is observed. There is no evidence of malignancy in the periduodenal lymph nodes.
- Specimen C (neck of pancreas) and G (uncinate process) both show no evidence of malignancy.
- Specimen O (bile duct) shows biliary epithelium with acute inflammation and focal reactive atypia, but no evidence of malignancy.
- The gallbladder shows chronic cholecystitis with no evidence of malignancy.
- Frozen sections performed on the adrenal mass, retroperitoneal lymph node, neck of pancreas, and bile duct, confirm the presence or absence of malignancy in these specimens.
- The clinical history provided is "pancreatic tumor," but the pre-operative and post-operative diagnoses are not provided.
- The gross description of the adrenal mass mentions that it is a cystic lesion measuring 4.4 cm, surrounded by a thin layer of tan-yellow tissue. The external surface appears smooth and black. There are papillary projections present, and a tissue fragment has been frozen for intraoperative diagnosis.
- The retroperitoneal lymph node gross description is not provided in the report.

This pathology report describes the findings from an adrenalectomy for a right adrenal pheochromocytoma. The tumor is well circumscribed, measuring 4 cm in maximum dimension, with no evidence of vascular invasion or necrosis. The specimen weighs 54.07 grams and has a red-tan soft tissue appearance. The cut surface of the tumor is homogeneous with a thin rim of yellow tissue around the periphery, which represents normal adrenal tissue. Approximately 50% of the tissue has been procured for further examination. No lymph nodes are grossly identified. Representative sections of the tumor and normal adjacent tissue have been submitted for analysis. The gross description and examination were conducted by a surgeon pathologist.

The pathology report describes a left adrenal gland resection that was performed for a patient diagnosed with a pheochromocytoma. The gross description of the specimen notes a red-tan ovoid nodule measuring 4.5 x 4.0 x 2.3 cm, as well as an attached fat fragment. The tumor nodules are inked black for identification. A small piece of the tissue is given for further testing, and the remainder is placed in formalin for processing. Additional adipose tissue adjacent to the adrenal gland is also received and preserved for research. The report does not provide any further details or findings from the microscopic examination or immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the right adrenal gland that is soft and necrotic, measuring 5 cm in diameter. Histologically, the tumor is characterized as a pleomorphic tumor with areas of zellballen and single giant cells present. There is no capsule surrounding the tumor. Immunohistochemical staining shows diffuse staining for synaptophysin and chromogranin, and focal staining for AE1/3. Sustentacular cells are identified by positive staining for S100. Only the adjacent adrenal parenchyma stains positive for MART1 and inhibin. The Ki67 proliferation index is 5%. The final diagnosis is pheochromocytoma.

Summary: The pathology report describes the excision of two nodules in the left adrenal gland of a 48-year-old female. The nodules are diagnosed as extra-adrenal paragangliomas, with one measuring 1.8 x 1.5 x 1.5 cm and the other measuring 1.3 x 0.8 x 0.8 cm. Margins are negative. The report also indicates that the patient has a history of pheochromocytoma and underwent a laparoscopic adrenal operation. The gross description of the excised tissue includes a well-circumscribed solid tan mass and a well-encapsulated, well-circumscribed mass filled with slightly gelatinous tissue.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the adrenal gland that is completely encapsulated and measures 5.5x4.5x4.5 cm with some areas of hemorrhage. There are no mitotic figures or necrosis, but there is a large fibrous scar. The tumor is well-capsulated and there is no evidence of vascular invasion. Samples taken from the normal adrenal cortex show no abnormalities or nodules. The report suggests that the tumor could be an adrenal paragangloma or pheochromocytoma. The PASS score and other details are not provided.

The pathology report describes the findings from a surgical resection of various tissues. 

1. A lymph node in the portahepatic region was removed and found to be reactive, with no evidence of tumor.
2. A retroperitoneal mass was resected and identified as a paraganglioma based on its histological features and immunohistochemical profile. The tumor cells were positive for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and CD58, and negative for inhibin and AE1/AE3. The tumor extended to the inked margin.
3. Another lymph node was resected, but no tumor was seen and there were only artifacts present.

Note: The immunohistochemistry performed on the tumor cells and the in-situ hybridization tests used for diagnosis were developed and validated by the Laboratory of Pathology. The laboratory is certified under the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) and is qualified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing.

The clinical history indicated a suspected paraganglioma and the specimen was taken for a specific protocol. Frozen sections were examined during the surgery and no tumor was found on the portahepatic lymph node.

The gross description of the specimens received includes the details of each sample and the procedures performed. The lymph node in the portahepatic region was a reddish-tan soft tissue node, while the retroperitoneal mass was a nodular tissue with a thin wispy tan capsule. The lymph nodes for permanent processing were tan-black-yellow soft tissue fragments.

No additional consultants were involved in the analysis.

The report also includes a disclaimer regarding the use of immunoperoxidase and in-situ hybridization tests, stating that they have not been cleared or approved by the FDA, but their use is permissible according to FDA regulations.

This pathology report summarizes the findings from a surgical procedure involving the spleen, colon, adrenal gland, kidney, pancreas, and soft tissue. 

The spleen was resected and showed no histologic abnormalities. 
The splenic flexure of the colon had no histologic abnormalities and there was no evidence of tumor involvement in the mesentery or omentum.
The left adrenal gland, left kidney, and distal pancreas were resected. In the adrenal gland, there was a malignant pheochromocytoma tumor measuring 20.0 cm that extended into the surrounding soft tissue, pancreas, and kidney. There was evidence of lymphovascular invasion. Surgical margins were negative. One lymph node showed no evidence of neoplasm.
The soft tissue in the retroperitoneum, which was excised, showed benign adipose tissue and no neoplasm.

Overall, the main finding was a malignant pheochromocytoma involving the adrenal gland, pancreas, and kidney, with lymphovascular invasion. The other organs and tissues examined did not show any significant abnormalities.

Summary:
The pathology report describes the examination of a periaortic mass and the left adrenal gland. The periaortic mass is described as a well-circumscribed, homogeneous mass without any areas of cystic degeneration or necrosis. Representative sections of the mass were submitted for further analysis. The left adrenal gland is also described as having a well-circumscribed solid mass that appears to arise from the medulla, with no areas of necrosis present. There is a rim of uninvolved adrenal gland surrounding the mass. Representative sections of the mass and adjacent adrenal gland were submitted for analysis. The report verifies the presence of paragangliomas in the periaortic soft tissue and pheochromocytomas in the left adrenal gland, with negative margins. The report states that the signing staff pathologist personally examined and interpreted the slides.

The pathology report describes a left adrenalectomy specimen from a patient with a known history of pheochromocytoma. The tumor mass is described as tan in color with fibrous adhesion on the capsular surface. It weighs 95.0 grams and measures 6.0 x 6.0 x 3.0 cm. The cut surface of the tumor is dark brown and solid, with diffuse cystic spaces ranging in size from 0.1 cm to 1.0 cm in diameter. Microscopically, the tumor is composed of large polygonal cells arranged in nests and trabeculae. The cells have a granular basophilic cytoplasm and oval/round nuclei. There is marked sinusoidal dilation in some areas, as well as focal areas of nuclear pleomorphism, hyaline globules, melanin pigment, and areas of hemorrhage. The tumor is synaptophysin, chromogranin, and S100 positive, consistent with the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. There is no evidence of lymphovascular invasion. Immunohistochemical stains for other markers are pending and will be reported separately.

This is a pathology report for a patient with a right thoracic paraganglioma. The report states that the margins of resection, including the inferior margins, lateral margin, and medial margin, are free of tumor. Two lymph nodes were examined and no tumor was seen. Additional testing showed that the tumor cells stained positively for chromogranin and synaptophysin. The report also mentions that the laboratory performing the tests is certified under CLIA to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing.

The pathology report describes a surgical specimen labeled as "right adrenal" that was received fresh. The specimen is a 19 gram portion of adrenal tissue with adherent fibroadipose tissue. The dimensions of the specimen are 10.0 x 3.0 x 1.1 cm. The adrenal gland itself measures 5.5 x 2.2 x 8 cm. Upon incision, there is a 1.6 x 1.6 x 1.1 cm mass that appears tan-white to pink in color. Surrounding the mass is a thin rim of orange cortex. There is also a small amount of normal adrenal tissue at one end of the specimen. Microscopic examination reveals a pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland with no evidence of capsular or vascular invasion or necrosis. Additional sections of the specimen have been saved for further analysis.

The pathology report confirms the diagnosis of a pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland. The adrenal medulla is completely replaced with neoplastic chromaffin cells, forming two nodules measuring 1.0 and 0.4 cm. There are neoplastic cells at the resection margin, which is expected in a cortical sparing adrenalectomy. The neoplastic cells show large nests and focal spindling, indicating potential malignant behavior, although there is no evidence of invasion or increased mitotic activity. Clinical correlation is required. The specimen received is a disrupted adrenal gland with cauterization artifact. The nodules are submitted for further examination.

The pathology report describes the findings of a surgical procedure on a patient with bilateral pheochromocytoma, which is a type of tumor in the adrenal glands. 

Specimen "A" refers to the left adrenal gland, which weighed 37 grams and measured 6.5 x 5.5 x 3.0 cm. The adrenal gland showed a well-circumscribed lobulated rubbery nodule measuring 4.2 x 3.3 x 2.2 cm, with a gold-yellow cut surface and a slightly hemorrhagic center. The nodule originated from the adrenal medulla and was close to the inked margin. The rest of the adrenal gland had a gold-yellow cortex and a brown-tan medulla. Representative sections were taken for further examination.

Specimen "B" refers to the right adrenal gland, which weighed 457 grams and measured 13.5 x 10.5 x 6.5 cm. The gland showed a solid mass with some attached yellow lobulated adipose tissue. The mass had a heterogeneous red-pink cut surface, with a solid area that was 90% solid and 10% cystic. The cystic component consisted of several smooth-walled unilocular cysts filled with brown-red thick fluid. The periphery of the mass contained remnants of adrenal gland cortex and medulla. Representative sections were taken for further examination.

The microscopic examination of both specimens was performed, but the report does not provide specific details of the findings.

Overall, the report confirms the presence of pheochromocytomas in both adrenal glands, with the left adrenal gland having a smaller tumor compared to the right adrenal gland.

This pathology report describes a surgical procedure to remove a left adrenal mass. The diagnosis of the mass is a pheochromocytoma, a benign tumor composed of small nests of cells within a vascular background. The tumor measures 3.2 cm in greatest dimension and shows salt-and-pepper chromatin, moderate cytologic pleomorphism, and rare multinucleation. There is no evidence of extra adrenal infiltration, vascular invasion, increased mitotic activity, or necrosis. The mass appears encapsulated and originated from the medulla of the adrenal gland. Portions of the tissue have been submitted for further analysis.

The pathology report describes a left adrenal tumor that is encapsulated and weighs 42 grams. The tumor has a soft consistency and pink-red color. Microscopically, it is identified as a pheochromocytoma with solid and alveolar patterns, along with focal hemorrhages. There is also evidence of Feyrter's metaplasia in the surrounding adrenal cortex. Immunohistochemical staining shows frequent sustentacular cells. The report also mentions several features associated with a pheochromocytoma, such as large nests or diffuse growth, central or confluent tumor necrosis, high cellularity, cellular monotony, tumor cell spindling, mitotic figures, atypical mitotic figures, extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, and capsular invasion. The date of procurement and confirmation are not provided in the report.

The pathology report describes a tumor consistent with a pheochromocytoma. The tumor is contained within a fibrous capsule and measures 130x100x90 mm and weighs 640 g. The tumor appears brown-yellow and spotted on gross examination. Microscopic examination reveals that the tumor is diffusely and solidly composed of alveolar-shaped cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, some of which are polygonal or spindle-shaped. There is evidence of fibrosis, lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, and both fresh and old hemorrhage. There is no invasion into blood vessels or through the capsule. The presence of adipose tissue surrounding the tumor could not be evaluated. Large foci of scarring are observed in the central part of the tumor. Immunohistochemical staining shows negative results for $100 protein, indicating a lack of sustentacular cells, and low positivity for MIBI. Congo red staining is negative. The tumor meets the criteria for a pheochromocytoma based on the PASS scoring system, with features such as large nests or diffuse growth, central tumor necrosis, high cellularity, cellular monotony, tumor cell spindling, and mitotic figures greater than 3 per 10 high-power fields. There is no evidence of extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, or capsular invasion. The tumor also exhibits profound nuclear pleomorphism and nuclear hyperchromasia. The procurement date and confirmation date are not provided in the report.

The pathology report describes two specimens: one from the right adrenal gland and one from the left adrenal gland. 

The right adrenalectomy specimen reveals a composite pheochromocytoma consisting of pheochromocytoma and ganglioneuroma. The entire gland is occupied by the tumor, so assessment of underlying adrenal medullary hyperplasia cannot be accurately performed.

The left adrenalectomy specimen shows a clear cell adrenal cortical adenoma with central degeneration. There is no evidence of adrenal medullary hyperplasia or atrophy of the non-tumorous adrenal cortex.

The report also mentions that at least 30% of pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas are associated with familial syndromes. The possibility of MEN2 syndrome is unlikely since there is no adrenal medullary hyperplasia in the nontumorous medulla (left adrenal). The tumor will be tested for SDHB expression, as loss of SDHB expression is a marker for familial paraganglioma syndromes caused by SDH mutations.

The gross description of the specimens is also mentioned in the report.

Overall, the report indicates the presence of a composite pheochromocytoma in the right adrenal gland and a clear cell adrenal cortical adenoma with degeneration in the left adrenal gland. Further testing for SDHB expression will be done to investigate the possibility of familial paraganglioma syndromes. No lymph node involvement or metastases were identified.

Summary:
The pathology report describes a surgical excision of a tumor in the left adrenal gland. The tumor is diagnosed as a pheochromocytoma, a rare tumor that arises from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. The lesion measures 2.7 cm and appears to be contained within the adrenal gland. Microscopic examination shows the tumor is comprised of spindled and epithelioid cells arranged in a classic nested pattern. There is no evidence of nuclear atypia, necrosis, or invasion of surrounding structures. The tumor cells show immunoreactivity for markers such as synaptophysin and chromogranin. The report mentions that a proliferation index test has been ordered to further evaluate the tumor. The gross description of the excised specimen notes disruption and friability of the mass, as well as areas of hemorrhage. Representative sections of the tumor and normal adrenal gland are submitted for further analysis.

The pathology report describes the findings from a biopsy of an inferior mesenteric vein lymph node and an adrenalectomy performed on a female patient. 

For the lymph node biopsy, the report states that no lymph node was identified, and the tissue was found to be benign fibroadipose tissue with no tumors seen.

For the adrenalectomy specimen, the report indicates the presence of an adrenal pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal gland, with atypical histologic features that raise concerns for possible malignant clinical behavior. The tumor measures 3.8 x 2.9 x 2.7 cm and shows vascular invasion, capsular invasion, peri-adrenal soft tissue involvement, and extension into peri-adrenal adipose tissue. These features suggest potential aggressive biologic behavior. Close clinical follow-up is recommended.

Special stains performed on the tumor confirm the diagnosis. The tumor shows diffuse reactivity for synaptophysin and chromogranin. Some disruption of the sustentacular cell network is observed, and moderate staining of tumor cells is seen with a stain called $-100.

The frozen section diagnosis of the adrenal gland tumor is confirmed. 

There is no mention of lymph node involvement or the presence of metastasis.

The report does not provide information about the patient's symptoms, prior imaging studies, or any other clinical history.

The pathology report indicates the presence of a tumor in the right adrenal gland. The tumor is confined to the adrenal gland and does not involve any surrounding tissues or organs. There are no significant abnormalities observed in the tumor clusters. The report also mentions that the tumor is consistent with a diagnosis of malignant pheochromocytoma, based on the presence of metastasis, which is considered a defining criterion.

The pathology report indicates that the patient underwent a laparoscopic right adrenalectomy for the removal of a pheochromocytoma, which is a 2 cm tumor located within the right adrenal gland. The tumor appears to be completely encapsulated and there is no evidence of lymph node involvement. The report states that the signing pathologist has personally examined and interpreted the slides from this case.

This is a pathology report for a pheochromocytoma, a tumor that arises from the adrenal glands. The tumor is ovoid and encapsulated, measuring 60x50x38 mm and weighing 55 g. It has a grey-pink color and a soft consistency. There are remnants of the adrenal cortex on the periphery, which show pressure atrophy. Microscopically, the tumor consists of large polygonal cells with focal hemorrhages. Adrenal cortex remnants are confirmed histopathologically, but in some areas they are completely eroded. There is no invasion behind the tumor capsule. Immunohistochemical examination shows the presence of sustentacular cells in some parts of the tumor, but staining for $100 protein is negative in other parts. The proliferation activity (MIB-1) is minimal, less than 1%. The tumor meets 4 out of the 12 criteria in the Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal Gland Scaled Score (PASS) system, including large nests or diffuse growth, central or confluent tumor necrosis, high cellularity, and cellular monotony. There is no evidence of extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, or capsular invasion.

The pathology report describes a left adrenal gland tumor measuring 80x50x50 mm and weighing 39 g. The tumor is thinly encapsulated and grey-pink in color. Microscopically, it is identified as a pheochromocytoma, which is a solidly alveolarly and trabecularly shaped tumor with significant fibrosis. The tumor invades under the fibrous capsule of the adrenal gland but does not infiltrate beyond it. Large foci of Feyrter's metaplasia are found in the periadrenal fat tissue. Sustentacular cells are present sporadically. The tumor shows a proliferation activity (MIB1) of 1-2%. Several characteristics are noted, including large nests or diffuse growth, central or confluent tumor necrosis, high cellularity, cellular monotony, tumor cell spindling, mitotic figures, atypical mitotic figure(s), extension into adipose tissue, vascular invasion, capsular invasion, nuclear pleomorphism, and total weight. The report does not provide the procurement date or confirmation date. The overall interpretation is "PASS."

The pathology report describes a case of a pheochromocytoma in the left adrenal gland. The tumor cells stained positive for S-100, NSE, Synatophysin, and CDSS, indicating a pheochromocytoma. Some sections also showed adrenal cortical tissue. The surgical procedure involved the removal of a large left-sided adrenal mass that was not invading surrounding structures. The pre-operative and post-operative diagnosis was pheochromocytoma. The gross description of the specimen revealed a yellow/red tissue measuring 7.6 x 8.8 x 6.9 cm, with a normal adrenal gland present along one aspect, and a brown/red soft nodule occupying the rest of the specimen. The nodule had a tan/red cut surface with punctate hemorrhages and a faint rim of normal-appearing adrenal tissue at the periphery. A small fragment of the nodule and normal tissue was procured for further analysis. The report concludes with a note that the immunoperoxidase tests performed were developed and their performance characteristics determined by the laboratory, which is certified to perform high complexity clinical laboratory testing.

The pathology report indicates that the patient underwent a left adrenalectomy. The final diagnosis of the specimen removed from the left adrenal gland is a pheochromocytoma, which is a tumor arising from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. The size of the tumor is 2.3x1.6x1 cm and it is confined to the adrenal gland. The margins of resection are free of tumor. The report also mentions that the adrenal cortex shows no specific pathological changes.

The pathology report describes a surgical specimen of an adrenal gland that was removed laparoscopically. The adrenal gland weighed 22 grams and had dimensions of 7 x 4 x 2 cm. A spherical lesion measuring 3.5 cm was found within the gland. The lesion was moderately defined by a pseudo-capsule and consisted of groups and trabeculae of moderately polymorphic cells with occasional zellballen and areas of hemorrhage. The cells had round oval nuclei, basophilic cytoplasm, and prominent nucleoli. There were also regions of highly polymorphic cells with large hyperchromatic, irregular nuclei and limited cytoplasm. No significant mitotic activity or necrosis was observed. No growth was seen in the surrounding fat. There was suspected vascular invasion in the local area. The resection borders were free, indicating complete removal of the lesion. The diagnosis of the lesion is pheochromocytoma.

The pathology report indicates that the patient had a radical cystoprostatectomy for the treatment of carcinoma. The report shows that there is transitional cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder, as well as adenocarcinoma of the prostate. There is also evidence of lymph node involvement, with multiple lymph nodes showing suspicion for metastasis. The report also mentions the presence of high-grade carcinoma and patchy areas of transitional cell carcinoma. The report concludes that there is no tumor seen at the surgical margins. Overall, the report provides detailed information about the type and extent of the carcinoma and lymph node involvement.

This is a pathology report for a patient with bladder cancer who underwent radical cystectomy (removal of the bladder), total hysterectomy (removal of the uterus), and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (removal of the fallopian tubes and ovaries). The report states that there is no malignancy seen in the left and right pelvic lymph nodes, appendix, and ureter margins. The tumor in the bladder is described as squamous type with extensive glandular differentiation and a size of 3.0 cm. It is invading the perivesical tissue and shows extensive perineural invasion. The tumor is classified as grade 3/3 and is staged as pT1a, pN0, pMX. The report also mentions benign findings such as atrophic endometrium, leiomyomata (fibroids), atrophic ovaries, and focal endosalpingiosis.

The pathology report indicates the following findings:

1. Distal margin of the urethra: High fibromuscular tissue, no evidence of cancer.
2. Left pelvic lymph nodes: 5 metastatic nodes out of several examined, high-grade urothelial carcinoma.
3. Right pelvic lymph nodes: 7 metastatic nodes out of several examined, high-grade urothelial carcinoma.
4. Radical cystectomy: Invasive urothelial carcinoma with diffuse growth pattern and focal micropapillary features, high grade. Invasion of perivesical soft tissues, involvement of prostatic stroma, vascular and perineural invasion. Tumor present at urethral margin, urothelial carcinoma in situ present at right ureteral margin.
5. Non-neoplastic mucosa: Chronic cystitis, foreign body reaction, proliferative cystitis. Nodular hyperplasia in the prostate. Involvement of seminal vesicles by urothelial carcinoma.
6. Vas deferens excisions: Benign tissue.
7. Ureteral stent removals: Ureteral stents in both left and right ureters.
8. Periureteral tissue excision: Invasive high grade urothelial carcinoma involvement.
9. Distal margin excision of the urethra: Invasive high-grade urothelial carcinoma involvement.
10. Distal left ureter excision: Benign tissue.

Based on the pathology report, the diagnosis includes:
- Soft tissue, ureteral margin, biopsy: No tumor seen
- Bladder and prostate, radical cystoprostatectomy:
   - Bladder:
      - Invasive high-grade urothelial carcinoma with squamous differentiation
      - Tumor size: 6.0 cm by gross examination
      - Invasion into perivesicular soft tissues
      - Unifocal tumor in left wall, anterior wall, trigone, and left ureterovesicular junction
      - Focal hemangiovascular space invasion identified; no definite lymphovascular space invasion
      - Associated urothelial carcinoma in situ
   - Ureters: Negative for tumor
   - Urethra: Negative for tumor
   - Paravesicular soft tissue: Negative for tumor, but close to the left lateral wall and right anterior wall (less than 0.1 cm)
   - Other findings in the bladder and prostate include chronic cystitis, benign prostatic hyperplasia, acute and chronic prostatitis, and no evidence of urothelial carcinoma in the prostate
- Prostate:
   - Prostatic adenocarcinoma with Gleason combined score 6 (3+3)
   - Approximately 2% of the right lobe involved by tumor
   - Confined within the prostatic capsule
   - No invasion of the seminal vesicles or lymphovascular spaces
   - Negative surgical margins in the prostate

The pathological stage is pT3b pNO for the bladder cancer. The assessment of the stage is subject to change pending clinical review and additional information.

This pathology report summarizes the findings of a urinary bladder cystectomy specimen. The diagnosis is transitional cell carcinoma, with a tumor size of 2.2cm and a papillary configuration. The tumor is located on the right and left walls of the bladder and has invaded the muscularis propria (detrusor muscle). There is no direct invasion of other organs or structures, and venous/lymphatic invasion is absent. All margins are negative for malignancy, and nearest margin is 5cm away. Lymph node dissections were performed and all sampled lymph nodes are found to be benign. The staging for primary tumor is pT2a, lymph nodes are pNO, and distant metastasis cannot be assessed. The clinical information indicates the patient has bladder cancer, and various specimens were received for analysis including ureter segments and lymph nodes. Frozen section analysis of the ureter margins and subsequent permanent sections reveal benign findings. The lymph nodes show partial replacement by adipose tissue and they range in size. Multiple lymph nodes are submitted in each specimen.

The pathology report describes the findings of a patient who underwent a radical cystectomy, total abdominal hysterectomy, and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (exenteration) for bladder cancer. The report includes findings from multiple biopsies and lymph node dissections.

The main findings are as follows:
A. Right ureter biopsy: No carcinoma identified
B. Left ureter biopsy: No carcinoma identified
C. Bladder: High-grade invasive urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, involving the muscularis propria. Focal carcinoma in situ. No carcinoma seen in pericystic lymph nodes.
D. Right pelvic lymph node dissection: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma found in 2 of 8 lymph nodes.
E. Left pelvic lymph node dissection: No carcinoma identified in 6 lymph nodes.
F. Final ureter, left biopsy: No carcinoma identified.
G. Final ureter, right biopsy: No carcinoma identified.

The synoptic comment on the bladder tumor describes the tumor type (urothelial carcinoma), grade (high-grade), size (4.0 cm), extent of invasion into the bladder wall, absence of lymphatic/vascular invasion, presence of carcinoma in situ, absence of tumor extension into adjacent organs, and negative margins.

The report concludes with the stage of the tumor (pT2bN2Mx) according to AJCC/UICC staging criteria.

Overall, the report confirms the presence of high-grade invasive urothelial carcinoma in the bladder, with metastasis to lymph nodes. It also rules out the presence of carcinoma in the ureters and provides information about the extent and characteristics of the tumor.

The pathology report indicates the following findings:

- Invasive high-grade urothelial carcinoma in the urinary bladder.
- Flat urothelial carcinoma in situ in the urinary bladder.
- The carcinoma invades 7.0 cm and extensively invades into the detrusor muscle and perivesicular soft tissue.
- Flat carcinoma in situ is present at the left ureter margin.
- Extensive lymphovascular invasion and perineural invasion are identified.
- Extensive tumor necrosis is present.
- Pathological stage is pT3a N1 MX.
- The prostate has benign prostatic hyperplasia and is negative for carcinoma.
- Metastatic urothelial carcinoma is found in one of six lymph nodes in the left pelvic area.
- Eight out of eight lymph nodes in the right pelvic area are benign.
- The final margin biopsy of the left ureter shows flat carcinoma in situ.
- The final margin biopsy of the right ureter shows benign urothelium with reactive changes.
- The tumor configuration is papillary and solid.
- The pathological staging is pT3b.
- The left ureter margin is involved by carcinoma.
- Venous/lymphatic vessel invasion is present.
- Direct extension of the invasive tumor into the perivesical fat is identified.
- Additional findings include urothelial carcinoma in situ and urothelial dysplasia (low-grade intraurothelial neoplasia).

This pathology report is for a patient who underwent radical cystectomy and prostatectomy for urothelial carcinoma. The report includes findings from lymph node dissection, bladder, prostate, bilateral vas deferens, and distal ureter excision.

The lymph nodes removed from the right pelvic region (18 nodes) and left pelvic region (8 nodes) did not show any tumor.

In the bladder, high grade urothelial carcinoma with sarcomatoid change was observed. The tumor was found to invade through the muscularis propria and into the perivesical fat. The prostate showed high grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia. No tumor was found in the perivesical lymph node. All specimen margins were free of tumor.

The distal ureter did not show any tumor.

The pathology report provides information on the type, grade, depth of invasion, distribution, margins, and lymph node status of the urothelial carcinoma. The TNM staging is pT3b,NO,MX, indicating a locally advanced tumor without lymph node involvement or distant metastasis.

Overall, the report suggests that the patient had urothelial carcinoma with sarcomatoid change in the bladder, but no evidence of tumor spread to the lymph nodes or other organs.

The pathology report indicates that the patient underwent an anterior pelvic exenteration, Studer pouch to urethra procedure, pelvic lymphadenectomy, and G-tube placement. 

The report shows that there is no high grade atypia or tumor identified in the bladder, uterus, bilateral ovaries and tubes, cervix, left distal ureter, left para aortic lymph nodes, and apical urethral margin.

However, in the bladder, there is invasive poorly differentiated urothelial carcinoma extending through the wall with clear margins. The tumor measures 3.5 x 3 x 1.8 cm and is graded as 3 & 4/4. It has spread into the perivesical soft tissues of the trigone, left lateral wall, and left ureterovesical junction. Lymphovascular invasion is identified, and there are foci of cystitis glandularis et cystica and mild to moderate urothelial dysplasia. There is no high grade dysplasia or urothelial carcinoma in situ (flat lesion) identified.

The lymph node analysis reveals metastatic carcinoma identified in two out of four left obturator/hypogastric lymph nodes, and in one out of four pre sacral lymph nodes. 

The overall pathologic TNM stage is pT3bw2MX.

The pathology report describes the findings from a surgical procedure involving the bladder and prostate. The microscopic examination reveals a poorly differentiated, invasive urothelial carcinoma. The tumor cells have a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, a high mitotic rate, and moderate nuclear pleomorphism. The tumor cells invade the prostatic tissue near the inked prostatic capsular radial margin. Other specimens received include ureteral margins, peritoneal mass, inferior urethral margin, and posterior urethral margin. The gross examination of the bladder and prostate specimen shows a lobulated mass with ulceration and necrosis, located at the interface between the bladder and prostate. The prostatic urethra is grossly involved, with excavation of the verumontanum. The bladder mucosa is edematous, and the uninvolved wall thickness is 0.6 cm. The maximum depth of invasion is 1.1 cm. Multiple sections of the specimen are submitted for further examination.

This pathology report describes the findings from a surgical procedure on a patient with bladder carcinoma. The specimens submitted include various lymph nodes, bladder tissue, prostate, seminal vesicles, urethra, and other surrounding tissues. 

The report indicates that the right pelvic lymph nodes and perivesical tissue excisions were benign, meaning there was no evidence of cancer. However, the right pelvic lymph nodes were involved in the cancer, with three lymph nodes examined and no metastasis detected. The left pelvic lymph nodes excision also showed no involvement or metastasis in the two nodes examined.

The bladder, prostate, seminal vesicles, urethra, perivesical tissue, and lymph nodes excision revealed invasive urothelial carcinoma, a high-grade tumor. The non-invasive component showed flat in situ carcinoma growth pattern, while the invasive component showed infiltrating growth pattern. The tumor did not exhibit multicentricity, and local invasion was limited to the superficial half of the muscularis propria. No extravesical tumor extension or vascular invasion was identified.

The surgical margins were free of tumor, and non-neoplastic mucosa exhibited granulomatous cystitis. The prostate showed nodular hyperplasia, while the seminal vesicles were not involved. The perivesical lymph nodes were not identified.

Based on the AJCC 2002 staging system, the pathologic stage was determined to be pT2a, indicating invasion of the superficial half of the muscularis propria without involvement of the prostate.

Other excised tissues, including the left and right vas deferens and the distal right ureter, were found to be benign without evidence of malignancy or metastasis.

In summary, the patient has bladder carcinoma with invasive urothelial carcinoma of high grade. The cancer involves the right pelvic lymph nodes, but not the left pelvic lymph nodes, with no evidence of metastasis in the lymph nodes examined. The tumor is limited to the bladder and superficial half of the muscularis propria without involvement of other organs or structures.

The following pathology report summarizes the findings of a surgical pathology report for a patient who underwent a bladder and prostate surgery. The report includes findings from various specimens received during the surgery.

1. Distal right ureter: The segment of the ureter is negative for carcinoma.

2. Distal left ureter: The segment of the ureter is benign and negative for dysplasia and malignancy.

3. Bladder and prostate: Invasive high-grade urothelial carcinoma is present, which has invaded the detrusor muscle and perivesical adipose tissue. The surgical resection margins are benign. There is no lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Lymph nodes do not show tumor presence. Scattered microscopic foci of high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia are present, but there is no involvement by transitional cell carcinoma. Seminal vesicles are unremarkable and do not show involvement by urothelial carcinoma.

The tumor is classified as Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, with a high-grade histologic grade. The tumor shows a papillary configuration for noninvasive elements and infiltrative configuration for invasive elements. Microscopic tumor extension is seen in the perivesical fat. The margins are uninvolved by invasive carcinoma. Lymph-vascular invasion is not identified. There are no additional pathologic findings.

The pathologic stage of the tumor is pT3a, pNO, PMX. The report also notes that the information on pathology stage and the operative procedure has been transmitted to the Institution's Cancer Registry for accreditation purposes.

The clinical history for the patient is bladder cancer.

Intraoperative consultations were performed for various specimens, including the distal right and left ureters, and the pelvic lymph nodes. No carcinoma was identified in these specimens.

Gross descriptions of the specimens received are provided, including the sizes and configurations of the specimens, as well as the attached structures.

Overall, the report indicates the presence of an invasive high-grade urothelial carcinoma in the bladder and prostate, with no involvement in the ureters or lymph nodes. Other associated findings are also mentioned.

The pathology report describes findings from a surgical procedure involving the bladder, prostate, and lymph nodes. The microscopic description reveals invasive transitional cell carcinoma (a type of bladder cancer) with a high grade and involvement of the muscularis propria, perivesical fat, soft tissue around the prostate, and seminal vesicles. Vascular space invasion and soft tissue deposits are identified. Focal prostatic adenocarcinoma (prostate cancer) with a Gleason score of 6 is also found in a specific region of the prostate. The urethra and surrounding tissue do not show signs of cancerous changes. Gross findings include measurements and descriptions of the bladder, prostate, ureters, and lymph nodes, as well as the presence of an ulcerated mass in the bladder. Sections of the specimens are submitted for further analysis.

The pathology report describes the findings from a bladder tumor excision and a left renal pelvis biopsy. 

For the bladder tumor excision (Specimen A), it is determined that there is a high grade papillary urothelial carcinoma that has invaded the muscularis propria. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion is identified. The tissue also shows areas of necrosis and calcification. 

For the left renal pelvis biopsy (Specimen B), there is a diagnosis of low grade papillary urothelial carcinoma. However, the report states that invasion cannot be assessed due to limited tissue sample. 

In summary, the report confirms a high grade papillary urothelial carcinoma in the bladder and a low grade papillary urothelial carcinoma in the left renal pelvis.

The pathology report describes the findings from a partial cystectomy procedure for a bladder tumor. The tumor is identified as a high-grade urothelial carcinoma with areas of clear cell differentiation. Invasion into the lamina propria is present, but there is no diagnostic invasive tumor identified in the sections of muscularis propria. Due to the nature of the tumor and the lack of orientation of the specimen, accurate margin evaluation is not possible.

This pathology report is for a patient who underwent cystectomy and prostatectomy for bladder cancer. The report includes findings from various specimens, including the distal right ureter, distal left ureter, urinary bladder/prostate, left pelvic lymph nodes, right pelvic lymph nodes, left ureter final margin, and right ureter final margin.

The summary of findings is as follows:
- Distal right ureter: No tumor found.
- Distal left ureter: No tumor found.
- Urinary bladder/prostate: Bladder with invasive high-grade urothelial carcinoma and prostatic adenocarcinoma with Gleason grade 3+3. One lymph node out of seven involved with metastatic urothelial carcinoma.
- Left pelvic lymph nodes: No tumor found in seven lymph nodes.
- Right pelvic lymph nodes: One lymph node out of seven involved with metastatic urothelial carcinoma.
- Left ureter final margin: No tumor found.
- Right ureter final margin: No tumor found.

Additional details such as gross description and clinical data are also included in the report.

The pathology report indicates the following findings:

1. No evidence of carcinoma in three lymph nodes from the right pelvic region.
2. No evidence of carcinoma in three lymph nodes from the left pelvic region.
3. Benign ureteral tissue found in a biopsy of the left ureter.
4. No evidence of carcinoma in the ureteral tissue.
5. Radical cystoprostatectomy was performed, removing the bladder, distal ureters, prostate, bilateral seminal vesicles, and bilateral vasa deferentia.
6. Carcinoma was found in the deep detrusor muscle of the bladder, with focal perineural invasion.
7. No evidence of angiolymphatic invasion identified.
8. No evidence of carcinoma in two lymph nodes from the right lac region.
9. The tumor is of high grade (grade 3) and infiltrating.

Overall, the report indicates the presence of carcinoma in the bladder and surrounding tissues, but no evidence of spread to the lymph nodes. The tumor is of high grade and has infiltrated into the deep muscle layer of the bladder.

This pathology report is for a 54-year-old male with T2 urothelial bladder cancer. The report includes information about the surgical procedures performed, including excision of left distal pelvic lymph nodes, cystoprostatectomy, and excision of left and right distal ureters. 

The report describes the findings of each procedure, including the presence of benign lymph nodes in both the left and right distal pelvic lymph nodes. The cystoprostatectomy showed invasive urothelial carcinoma, high grade with inverted and infiltrating growth pattern. Vascular invasion and perineural invasion were identified, but the surgical margins were free of tumor. Non-neoplastic mucosa exhibited proliferative cystitis, and nodular hyperplasia was seen in the prostate. The soft tissue around the seminal vesicles showed involvement by tumor, and tumor emboli were present in lymphovascular spaces. Perivesical lymph nodes were not identified.

The report concludes that the pathologic stage of the tumor is TS (invasion of perivesicle soft tissue) with PR? (periprostatic or periseminal vesicle soft tissue invasion). The ureters were found to be benign.

The pathology report describes a bladder sample that shows invasive urothelial carcinoma. The tumor cells are hyperplastic and form nests or groups. The cells have moderate and eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, enlarged nuclei with irregular nuclear membranes, nucleoli, and abnormal chromatin patterns. Mitoses are present. The tumor invades the muscle propria or nerves. The diagnosis is high-grade infiltrating urothelial carcinoma involving the muscularis propria.

Additional details include a cystectomy specimen with a tumor size of 5x4 cm and poorly differentiated transitional cell carcinoma histologic type. There is evidence of extracapsular extension but no lymph node involvement. The report does not specify the status of margins or evidence of neo-adjuvant treatment. There is no discrepancy between the pathology report and Case Quality Control Form.

The pathology report indicates that there was infiltration of a small-cell urothelial carcinoma in the cystectomy preparation. The tumor measured a maximum of 4.5 cm and showed microscopic infiltration of the perivesical fatty tissue and tumor infiltration of the lymph vessels. The tumor is at least 8.0 cm in size and invades through the detrusor muscle, extensively involving perivesicular adipose tissue. The carcinoma is also present at the perivesical adipose tissue resection margin. Focal carcinoma in-situ of both ureters is present as well. The urethral margin is free of in-situ or invasive malignancy. Extensive angiolymphatic invasion and focal perineural invasion are identified. The vaginal wall is free of tumor. The pathologic stage is pTNM = O73h.M1 Mx. There is also an incidental benign leiomyoma (0.8 cm) in the perivesical adipose tissue.

In the lymph nodes of the right pelvic, one out of two lymph nodes examined shows metastatic urothelial carcinoma. In the lymph nodes of the left pelvic, six out of seven lymph nodes examined show metastatic urothelial carcinoma.

The comment section states that the left ureteral resection margin shows mild urothelial atypia, which may represent low-grade intraurothelial neoplasia (dysplasia). There is no evidence of carcinoma in situ or invasive carcinoma at the margin. The report also includes synoptic data for primary urinary bladder tumors, pathologic staging as pT30, and information about margins and venolymphatic invasion.

Overall, the report indicates the presence of invasive urothelial carcinoma in the bladder with involvement of perivesical adipose tissue and lymph node metastasis. The report also mentions focal carcinoma in-situ in both ureters but no evidence of involvement in the urethral margin or vaginal wall.

This pathology report describes the examination of various tissues. 

In the lymph nodes, there were nine benign lymph nodes found.

In the ureter (right and left distal), there were benign urothelium and underlying submucosa with reactive changes observed.

In the prostate, bladder, seminal vesicles, vas deferens, radical cystectomy specimen, there was a 4.5 cm high-grade urothelial carcinoma present. The carcinoma involved the left lateral wall and extended into the detrusor muscle and perivesical soft tissue. Flat carcinoma in situ (CIS) component was identified, but there was no lymphovascular or perineural invasion.

In the prostate, focal high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) and non-neoplastic prostate with benign prostatic hyperplasia were observed.

The small cell carcinoma component in the bladder showed histological and cytological characteristics of small cell carcinoma. Immunostaining confirmed the neuroendocrine differentiation of the small cell component.

The tumor size of the bladder was 4.7 cm in its greatest dimension, and it was classified as a solid/nodular high-grade urothelial carcinoma.

No involvement of margins by invasive carcinoma, venous/lymphatic vessel invasion, direct extension of invasive tumor, or other associated epithelial lesions were found. Urothelial carcinoma in situ was also identified.

The pathology report indicates that the patient has a bladder tumor that is a high-grade (grade 3) urothelial carcinoma. The tumor has extensively invaded the lamina propria and muscularis mucosae, but there is no definitive evidence of invasion into the muscularis propria. The gross description of the tumor suggests that it is a 6.3 x 5.0 x 1.8 cm aggregate of pink-tan, soft, rubbery tissue fragments. The clinical history of the patient is bladder cancer.

The final diagnosis of the pathology report is as follows:

1. Right distal ureter: Frozen section showed no high grade atypia or tumor identified. No urothelial dysplasia or malignancy identified.

2. Para-aortic lymph nodes proximal limits: Benign.

3. Urethral margin: Frozen section showed no high grade atypia or tumor identified. Benign urethral and perithurethral tissue. No urothelial dysplasia or malignancy identified.

4. Bladder and prostate: Bladder shows in situ and invasive poorly differentiated transitional cell carcinoma, grade 4/4. Lymphovascular space invasion identified. Presence of reactive changes, mild, moderate, and severe urothelial dysplasia, and urothelial carcinoma in situ. Resection margins free of urothelial dysplasia and malignancy. Prostate shows unilateral/unifocal moderately differentiated prostatic adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 6, confined to the prostate gland without involvement of surrounding tissue.

5. Para-aortic lymph nodes: No metastatic carcinoma identified in two lymph nodes examined.

6. Common iliac, paracaval, external iliac, and obturator lymph nodes: No metastatic carcinoma identified in a total of 17 lymph nodes examined.

7. Presciatic lymph nodes: No metastatic carcinoma identified in three lymph nodes examined.

8. Presacral lymph nodes: No metastatic carcinoma identified in four lymph nodes examined.

9. Left presciatic lymph nodes: Benign fibropatty tissue, no lymphoid tissue or malignancy identified.

10. Proximal ureters: Benign hydroureter identified, no urothelial dysplasia or malignancy.

The pathological TNM stage of the bladder tumor is pT2a and the prostate tumor is pT2a. The report also mentions that a concurrent review of the patient's previous biopsy is being done, and results of a p53 assay will be reported separately.

It is a grade 3 & 4 carcinoma involving the superficial muscularis wall with focal carcinoma in situ. Focal adenomatous hyperplasia was seen in the prostate, but no high grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) or malignancy was identified. Chronic nonspecific inflammation was also observed in the prostate. The seminal vesicles and vasa deferentia showed no significant histopathologic change.

Overall, the pathological tumor stage is pT2aNoMx, and additional p52 molecular characterization is pending.

This pathology report describes a case of urothelial carcinoma, a type of bladder cancer, in a 26-year-old female. The report includes findings from surgical biopsies of the ureter margins and a radical cystoprostatectomy (removal of the bladder and prostate). 

The pathology report shows that there was no tumor seen in the ureter margins during the biopsies. However, in the bladder and prostate specimens, a high-grade urothelial carcinoma was found. The tumor measured 4 cm in size and had invaded through the muscle layer of the bladder into the surrounding fatty tissue. The tumor was located on the posterior wall, left lateral wall, and trigone of the bladder.

The report also notes the presence of extensive angiolymphatic space invasion, which indicates the potential for spreading to other parts of the body. The ulceration of the invasive cancer is also mentioned.

In terms of lymph node involvement, metastatic urothelial carcinoma was found in a total of 6 out of 41 lymph nodes. The largest lymph node metastasis was 2.5 cm in size and located in a perivesicular lymph node on the left side. Extracapsular extension, meaning the tumor had spread beyond the lymph node capsule, was also noted.

The pathology report includes information about the prostate as well, indicating the presence of adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 6 (3+3). However, the involvement of the prostate was minimal, with less than 5% of the prostate affected. There was no invasion into the seminal vesicles, and the surgical margins were free of prostate cancer.

Based on these findings, the pathologic TNM stage is determined to be pT3b pN2, indicating a locally advanced tumor with lymph node involvement.

The report also mentions the presence of benign prostatic hyperplasia, a non-cancerous condition of the prostate.

In summary, this pathology report describes a case of high-grade urothelial carcinoma in the bladder, with extensive invasion into surrounding tissue and lymph node involvement. It also notes the presence of adenocarcinoma in the prostate, but with minimal involvement.

The pathology report indicates that a radical cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection was performed, along with bowel resection for a right colon pouch with augmentation and G-tube placement. This pathology report is from a radical cystectomy procedure for a G3 pT2 ureteric carcinoma. The report includes findings from various specimens, including right ureteric margin, bladder and prostate tissue, lymph nodes, and surgical resection margins.
