Microscopy findings show a poorly differentiated solid transitional cell carcinoma that arises from dysplastic urothelium and invades through the muscle. There is no evidence of vascular or perineural invasion. The tumor is also seen to extend into the prostatic ducts and invade the prostate, but the prostatic margin is morphologically normal with normal surviving prostatic glands. The urethral surgical margin shows evidence of carcinoma in situ and invasive carcinoma. The background bladder tissue shows normal urothelium without dysplasia or carcinoma in situ. 

Concerning lymph nodes, there is a focus that appears to be part of a lymph node with possible invasion by urothelial carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry has been requested for further evaluation. The right ureteric margin shows focal carcinoma in situ, while the left ureteric margin shows carcinoma in situ of the urothelium. 

In summary, the findings indicate a poorly differentiated solid transitional cell carcinoma invading the prostate with regional node metastases. There is also background carcinoma in situ and involvement of the urethral and left ureteric surgical margins.

The carcinoma involves most of the urinary bladder, including the trigone, bilateral ureteral ostia, anterior and posterior walls, and right and left lateral walls. Overall, the report suggests the presence of invasive urothelial carcinoma in the urinary bladder with involvement of the ureters and lymph nodes. The tumor has invaded the detrusor muscle, perivesical adipose tissue, and shows rare perineural invasion and lymphatic tumor emboli. No other significant abnormalities are reported.

Additionally, there was urothelial carcinoma in situ involving the surface urothelium and von Brunn's nests. The report also mentions extensive cystitis cystica (formation of cysts in the bladder lining) and a small component of Gleason grade 5 (an indicator of the aggressiveness of prostate cancer) in the prostate adenocarcinoma. Extraprostatic extension (spread of cancer outside the prostate) was present, and the surgical margins were positive for carcinoma. The seminal vesicles and vas deferens did not show any tumor presence. The report also notes the presence of high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN), which is a precursor to prostate cancer. The remaining distal ureter did not show any tumor. The report provides staging information according to the TNM system for both bladder and prostate cancer. The comment section discusses the presence of a metastatic carcinoma in one lymph node and notes that an immunohistochemical stain for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) was non-contributory due to the absence of the malignant gland in the submitted section for analysis. The report was performed by the attending pathologist and reviewed with the clinical history of the patient.

This pathology report describes the findings from a surgical pathology examination of a patient with bladder cancer. The report notes the presence of invasive high-grade urothelial carcinoma in the bladder, as well as areas of urothelial atypia and focal papillary urothelial carcinoma. The tumor is found to invade into the vaginal wall and shows signs of vascular invasion. Lymph nodes in both the left and right pelvic regions are negative for metastatic carcinoma. The report also mentions the presence of extensive necrosis and suggests focal neuroendocrine differentiation within the tumor. The margins of resection are negative for tumor, except for the distal urethral margin which shows high-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma without invasion. Overall, the report provides detailed information about the extent and characteristics of the tumor. Immunohistochemical stains were performed to further characterize the tumor.

The pathology report indicates the following findings:

- Right distal ureter biopsy: Segment of benign ureter, no carcinoma or dysplasia seen
- Left distal ureter biopsy: Segment of benign ureter, no carcinoma or dysplasia seen
- Urinary bladder and prostate, radical cystoprostatectomy: Invasive high-grade urothelial carcinoma, involving the muscularis propria and anterior bladder wall, tumor measures 4.7 cm in greatest dimension. Surgical margins are free of carcinoma and dysplasia. Lymph nodes negative for metastatic carcinoma. Pathologic stage: pT2b NO Mx.
- Bladder with acute and chronic inflammation, reactive urothelial atypia, cystitis cystica, and focal intestinal metaplasia.

- Urethral margin with patchy necrosis, acute inflammation, and reactive urothelial atypia.
- Lymph nodes: Right pelvic lymph nodes (0/7), left common iliac and presacral lymph nodes (0/4), left pelvic lymph nodes (0/8) negative for metastatic carcinoma.
- Ancillary studies not done, but blocks available for additional studies if needed.

In summary, the report shows the presence of invasive urothelial carcinoma in the bladder and prostate, with no involvement of the ureters or lymph nodes. The surgical margins are clear. In addition, there are findings of inflammation and atypical changes in various tissues.

The pathology report indicates that the patient has invasive urothelial carcinoma, high grade, with squamous differentiation. The carcinoma measures 5.0 cm in size and extensively involves the perivesical adipose tissue. The surgical resection margins are positive in the right lateral and posterior regions. Perineural invasion and angiolympathic invasion are identified. There is no evidence of metastatic carcinoma in the lymph nodes examined. The appendix is benign and unremarkable. This pathology report describes a case of invasive high-grade urothelial carcinoma in the urinary bladder. The distal ureteral margins were negative for tumor. The TNM staging indicates pT4a, NO, MX. The report also includes a gross description of the specimens received.

The pathology report is describing a case of high grade papillary urothelial carcinoma that has infiltrated the bladder wall and extended into the prostate. Lymph nodes in the left obturator, left iliac, right obturator, and right iliac regions all show no presence of cancer cells. The report does not provide any additional information about the patient or their condition.

The pathology report shows that a radical cystectomy with continent urinary diversiom was performed. The frozen section diagnosis indicated negative results for the right ureter and urethral margin. The final diagnosis revealed benign prostatic glandular and stromal tissue with no evidence of malignancy. The bladder had invasive urothelial carcinoma that had invaded the muscularis propria but did not reach the inked margin. There was lymphovascular space invasion and no flat lesion (carcinoma in situ) identified. The prostate contained a microscopic focus of prostatic adenocarcinoma. The final pathologic stage was determined to be T3aNoMx for the bladder and T2aNOMK for the prostate.

This pathology report describes the findings from a radical cystoprostatectomy procedure. 

In the left ureter, a segment of benign ureter is identified.

In the lymph nodes, both right and left pelvic lymph nodes are found to be benign and negative for malignancy.

In the urinary bladder and distal ureters, ulgerated, invasive urothelial carcinoma (high-grade) is present. There is also flat urothelial carcinoma in situ within the bladder and prostatic urethra. One lymph node is found to have metastatic urothelial carcinoma, but without extracapsular extension.

In the prostate, adenocarcinoma is identified with a maximum dimension of 0.6 cm. The tumor has a Gleason score of 7 (primary Gleason grade 3, secondary Gleason grade 4). There is no extraprostatic extension, but perineural invasion is present. No seminal vesicle invasion is seen and all surgical margins are free of tumor. A total of 6 lymph nodes are examined, with 9 positive for tumor.

Overall, the report indicates the presence of invasive urothelial carcinoma in the bladder and distal ureters, and adenocarcinoma in the prostate. metastasis in one lymph node.

The pathology report describes the specimens received for analysis, including the left and right ureters, bladder, tubes, ovaries, vaginal wall, and lymph nodes in various locations. The pathology report indicates that a chstectomy with urinary diversion was performed. The report provides a final diagnosis of benign ureter with no urothelial dysplasia or malignancy identified. This pathology report indicates that the patient had a pre-operative diagnosis of bladder cancer, but the final diagnosis after surgery was uncertain (sema). The pathology report describes a bladder tumor that was removed during endoscopy. The tumor is classified as papillary urothelial carcinoma, moderately differentiated, and low-grade. There are areas of squamous metaplasia, ulceration, and necrosis. The tumor is classified as stpT1 (at least). 

A piece of cystoprostatectomy also shows a tumoral proliferation in the bladder with intramural evolution and invasion of the entire bladder wall. - No evidence of lymphatic or venous invasion.
- Uninvolved margins.
- No evidence of neo-adjuvant treatment.
- No additional pathologic findings.

Overall, the report describes the presence of bladder tumors with invasive characteristics and involvement of adjacent tissues, lymph nodes, and the bladder wall.

This pathology report describes a case of invasive urothelial carcinoma involving the bladder and prostate. The report states that there is no evidence of tumor in the lymph nodes or distal ureters. However, perineural invasion by carcinoma is observed in the neurovascular bundle. The tumor is described as high grade with squamous and glandular differentiation. It has invaded the prostatic stroma, seminal vesicles, and lymph nodes. The tumor extends to the margins of the extravesical and extraprostatic soft tissue. There is also evidence of urothelial dysplasia and carcinoma in situ in the urinary bladder and prostate. Frozen sections were performed on the ureters and neurovascular bundles. No tumor was seen in the ureters, but the neurovascular bundles showed highly atypical cells suspicious for carcinoma. The overall stage of the tumor is pT4a, indicating extensive local invasion.

The pathology report indicates that the specimen obtained was a distal right ureteric resection margin and lymph nodes. Various lymph nodes were examined, including the right obturator, left obturator, right external iliac, right internal iliac, and right sub-umbilical nodes. The macroscopic examination revealed cream-colored tissue, fatty tissue containing lymph nodes of different sizes, and grey tissue. The final staging was pT2b, pNO, R0.

The pathology report states that the patient underwent a transurethral resection of a bladder tumor, which was found to be a high grade papillary urothelial carcinoma with invasive features. Approximately 5% of the tumor exhibited a micropapillary pattern. In addition, benign urothelium with chronic inflammation was found in the prostatic urethra, along with chronic prostatitis and stromal nodule carcicinoma. No evidence of urothelial dysplasia or malignancy was identified. Vascular invasion was confirmed through staining.

The pathology report shows that the specimen taken from a cystectomy surgery includes the bladder, prostate, perivesicular fat, and ureteric stumps. The bladder shows a poorly differentiated (Grade 3) urothelial carcinoma, with invasion into the muscularis propria and extravesical fat. There is no evidence of lymphovascular invasion. The background bladder urothelium shows cystitis, but no metaplasia, dysplasia, or intraepithelial neoplasia. The ureteric and urethral resection margins are free of tumor. The closest peripheral surgical margin is 11 mm on the left side. The prostate gland contains extensive prostatic microacinar adenocarcinoma, with perineural involvement within the capsule but no extracapsular tumor. The prostatic adenocarcinoma has been fully excised with no evidence of tumor at intraprostatic or extraprostatic surgical resection margins. Metastatic urothelial carcinoma is found in some lymph nodes, but metastatic prostatic adenocarcinoma is found in two nodes. The summary diagnosis is Grade 3 urothelial carcinoma in the bladder and bilateral adenocarcinoma in the prostate.

The pathology report describes the findings from a cystoprostatectomy specimen of a male patient with high-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma of the bladder. There is also chronic and granulomatous inflammation consistent with treatment effect. The distal right ureter does not have any tumor. The report provides details about the tumor type, grade, depth of invasion, tumor distribution, margins, lymph nodes involvement, and the overall pathologic stage.

The pathology report shows that the patient underwent a partial hepatectomy for a well-defined mass in the liver, which was diagnosed as hepatic cellular carcinoma (HCC) with a moderate degree of differentiation and a trabecular histologic type. The margins of the resected liver tissue were not involved grossly, and there was no evidence of invasion of the surrounding tissues or organs. The remaining liver tissue was found to be cirrhotic. The pathology report describes a liver biopsy from a patient with a clinical diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The sample was obtained from a 5.0 x 4.2 x 3.9 cm pale tan, solid, and encapsulated mass located in the right posterior section of the liver. The tumor is hepatocellular in type, with a Trabecular and tubular histologic pattern. Edmondson-Steiner grade for the tumor is I, indicating low grade malignancy. No invasion into surrounding tissues or structures was observed, and the surgical resection margins were clear. Chronic hepatitis, likely caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV), was seen in the surrounding liver tissue. No cirrhosis was observed.

The report describes a tumor in the left lobe of the liver that is moderately-differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma with necrosis. The tumor cells are arranged in trabecular or sheet patterns, have large hyperchromatic nuclei and prominent nucleoli, and contain moderate cytoplasm. Mitoses are present. The stroma is marked fibrous and there is evidence of vascular invasion. The margins are uninvolved. No information is provided on lymph node or venous invasion or neo-adjuvant treatment.

This pathology report describes the following findings:

There is no evidence of vascular invasion. Surgical margins (edges) are clear of tumor. The background liver shows chronic hepatitis C with bridging fibrosis and early cirrhosis.

Additional information: Reticulin and trichrome stains confirm the above diagnosis.

It is important to consult a doctor for further clarification and treatment options based on these findings.

The report describes an excision product of a liver segment with a 6.5 cm diameter whitish and friable lesion identified as hepatocellular carcinoma of hepatic type. The surgical margin was 0.59 cm and there was moderate periportal fibrosis in the non-neoplastic liver tissue. No angiolymphatic invasion was detected and Schistosoma mansoni eggs were not observed. The pathological staging was pT1 (TNM - 7th edition).

The pathology report describes a liver resection for a patient with hepatocellular carcinoma. The tumor, classified as Grade 2, is a single mass measuring 4.2 x 3.8 x 3.2 cm and is located in liver segments II and III. The tumor has partially involved the hepatic capsule but has not invaded adjacent organs. The surgical margins are free of tumor, with a clearance of 2.5 cm. There is no extratumoral vascular invasion. The non-neoplastic liver tissue shows end-stage micronodular cirrhosis with steatosis and chronic inflammation. Overall, the tumor is classified as T2NX.

The pathology report describes a partial resection and wedge resection of two masses located in the liver, one in segment 3 and one in segment 7. The resection margins are not involved. The remaining liver parenchyme shows cirrhosis and mild mixed steatosis. The pathology report describes the examination of a gastrohepatic lymph node and a left lateral segment of the liver in a patient with suspected liver cancer. There is some mild non-specific chronic portal inflammation and lipid accumulation in the background hepatic parenchyma, but no significant background steatosis or iron accumulation is identified. The two examined gastrohepatic lymph nodes are negative for malignancy.

The pathology report describes a liver resection surgery for a hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The report also includes the gross description of the resected liver tissue.

The pathology report describes a case of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in segments 5 and 8 of the liver, which were surgically removed. The tumor in segment 5 was much smaller (2.2 x 2.0 x 2.0 cm) and had an encapsulated, pale green to tan mass with extensive necrosis and hemorrhage. It also had multinodular growth but did not invade any surrounding tissues. The report also notes that there was cirrhosis in the remaining liver tissue. Additionally, a chronic cholecystitis with cholesterolosis was observed in the gallbladder.

The pathology report describes a resected liver segment consisting of a well-differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma mass. The surgical resection margins are clear. The report also mentions the use of a reticulin stain, which showed loss of the reticulin framework in the carcinoma.

The report describes a moderately-differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma located in a lobe of the liver, with a size of 6x6x4cm and focal necrosis. The tumor cells exhibit various patterns and retain polygonal shape with round vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Mitoses are present. The margins are uninvolved and there is no evidence of neo-adjuvant treatment. No additional pathological findings are noted.

The pathology report shows that the patient has a mixed hepatocellular/cholangiocarcinoma in the left lobe of the liver, with moderate differentiation, multifocality, and vascular invasion. The tumor is confined to the liver with positive surgical margins. Lymph node status is negative, and the estimated total tumor diameter of all HCC foci is greater than 12 cm. Immunoperoxidase and special stains confirm the diagnosis and show staining patterns in tumor cells. The report also notes that the patient presented with left upper quadrant pain and a left-sided liver mass.

The pathology report describes a 6.0 cm sized hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in the right posterior segment (S6-7) of the liver, with a well-defined large round mass and a small multinodular confluent mass. The HCC is well-differentiated according to the Edmondson-Steiner grading system with trabecular histologic type and hepatic cell type. The report suggests the possibility of intrahepatic metastasis and multicentric occurrence, but this was not reported. The lymph node biopsy showed reactive hyperplasia. The final diagnosis includes HCC in the right hemihepatectomy, well-differentiated (Edmondson-Steiner grade 2), and autolysis with cholesterol polyps and cholelithiasis in the gallbladder.

The pathology report indicates that the patient underwent surgery to remove a tumor in the left lobe of the liver. The tumor is diagnosed as grade 2 hepatocellular carcinoma and measures 10.5 x 10.1 x 8.1 cm. It is located 1.8 cm away from the closest surgical margin. The rest of the liver tissue is normal. Additionally, a separate specimen from the right pelvic sidewall was also examined, which showed a leiomyoma measuring 7 mm in size.

The pathology report indicates that there is a primary tumor in the liver, which has metastasized to the lymph nodes, but there is no evidence of distant metastasis. The histological pattern of the tumor is diffuse, with necrosis and lymphocytic infiltration. There is no glandular cell differentiation, but there is evidence of round cell and large cell differentiation. The tumor shows nuclear atypia, aniso nucleosis, and hyperchromatism. The nuclear grade is not specified. The tumor is negative for estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR), but positive for Her-2/neu. The T-cell marker is negative, and other markers are also negative. The grade of the tumor is not specified. The histological diagnosis is adenocarcinoma. The report also mentions various histological features such as mosaic, stromal fibrosis, vascular invasion, and alveolar formation. Overall, the report suggests a primary liver adenocarcinoma with metastasis to the lymph nodes.

The pathology report describes a moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma in the left lobe of the liver, with negative margins of resection but positive vascular invasion. A portion of the tumor and normal parenchyma are submitted for tissue procurement, and there is no additional mass lesion or abnormality in the liver parenchyma. A pale firm focus measuring 3 cm in greatest dimension is noted at the margin, in keeping with cautery artifact. The report notes that the tumor is hepatocellular carcinoma, NDS, and the site is classified as liver CAR.

The pathology report identifies the findings from various tissue samples taken from the patient during surgery. The margins of resection are clear of tumor by at least 1 cm, and there is no evidence of vascular invasion. The remaining liver tissue is found to be noncirrhotic.

A biopsy of the diaphragm reveals a calcified fibrous nodule, which is also non-cancerous.

This pathology report describes a segment V resection of the liver, which revealed a moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma. The noninvolved parts of the liver showed macro and microsteatosis. The tumor was lobulated and subcapsular, measuring 1x9x7 cm. The tumor had less than 10% necrosis and did not show angiotymphatic invasion. The parenchymal margin was free of tumor. The pathological stage was determined to be Stage 1 (T1NxMx). The liver away from the carcinoma showed preserved normal framework and no increase in fibrosis or iron deposit. The frozen section diagnosis confirmed that the perpendicular margin was free of tumor. The gross description of the specimen noted a pink-tan to red-brown, hemorrhagic, and bosselated capsule. The tumor mass was irregular and ill-defined, with areas of necrosis and hemorrhage. Representative sections of the tumor, as well as additional sections of the specimen, were submitted for further examination.

The pathology report describes the findings from a surgical pathology examination. The main findings are as follows:

Overall, the report indicates that the patient has hepatocellular carcinoma with multiple tumor nodules in the liver and metastatic carcinoma in a lymph node. The tumor is moderately to poorly differentiated and there is extensive venous invasion. The surgical margins are positive for carcinoma. There are also findings of chronic cholecystitis with cholelithiasis in the gallbladder.

The patient's clinical diagnosis is hepatocellular carcinoma with rupture. The gross specimen is a liver with a tumor size of 11.0 x 9.0 x 8.0 cm and 10-20% tumor necrosis and hemorrhage/peliosis. The pathology report describes a liver mass measuring 16.5 x 12.0 cm, which was diagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with trabecular histologic type and the worst and major differentiation at grade II. The report describes a liver tumor with a clinical diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma. The pathology report is for a partial hepatectomy specimen from a patient with chronic hepatitis C infection and blood transfusion history. The patient underwent a liver resection, pericholedochal lymph node excision, and cholecystectomy. The pathology report shows that there is a hepatocellular carcinoma with focal sarcomatous differentiation in the liver posterior segmentectomy, which is a tumor with nodular growth and perinodular extension. The pathology report describes a case of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) located in the right lobe of the liver, with no invasion of bile ducts, hepatic vein, or hepatic artery. The pathology report describes a liver specimen from a patient with a history of hepatitis C who underwent a right partial hepatectomy of segment 7 due to a 9.5 mm hepatocellular carcinoma. The report describes a surgical pathology report for a patient with hepatocellular carcinoma in the left lateral segment of the liver. The pathology report describes a partial hepatectomy for a well-demarcated, nodular hepatic mass that was found to be hepatocellular carcinoma. This pathology report describes the findings from a surgical procedure on the liver. The biopsy of the right lobe of the liver showed benign (non-cancerous) tissue.

The pathology report describes a 15 cm pedunculated tumor in the left lateral (segment III) of the liver, diagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with variable histologic grades. The report also notes multifocality with a satellite tumor approaching but not transsected at the parenchymal margin. Vascular and transcapsular invasion are not present, and the tumor is organ-confined. The report includes information about margins tested and findings of steatosis, Mallory hyaline, triaditis, and peliosis. The AJC stage is noted as Stage IIIA; pT3a. A representative section of the tumor was submitted for issue banking. The report includes comments on the palliative resection to relieve gastric compression and evolution from well-differentiated adenoma-like HCC to moderately differentiated HCC.

The pathology report states that the patient had a left hemihepatectomy due to a well-defined yellow to tan nodule in the liver, and the diagnosis is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a type of liver cancer. The tumor is well-differentiated, with trabecular and pseudoglandular histologic type and microvessel invasion. The surgical resection margin was not involved, and there were no satellite nodules or serosal or portal vein invasion. The remaining parenchyma had stage 2 fibrosis. This pathology report describes the findings of a surgical biopsy and partial hepatectomy of a liver segment 4 lesion. The diagnosis is hepatocellular carcinoma, moderately differentiated. The report states that there are three nodules in the liver, measuring 1.5 cm, 8 cm, and 11 cm. The margins are negative for carcinoma, but there is a foreign body giant cell reaction to foreign material, possibly related to a history of embolization. The report also notes non-specific mild lymphocytic portal infiltrate and minimal steatosis in the uninvolved liver tissue. The pathology report describes a liver tumor that is moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma. The tumor invades vessels and normal hepatic tissue, and multiple tumors are present. The pathology report indicates that the specimen is liver tissue obtained through left lateral sectionectomy due to a suspected hepatocellular carcinoma. The gross examination showed a well-defined pale tan solid nodule in the liver. Microscopic examination confirmed the diagnosis of poorly differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma with Edmonson-Steiner grade 3/4 and trabecular and pseudoglandular histologic type. Mild fatty change and partial fibrous capsule formation were observed, as well as microvessel invasion and septal fibrosis. The pathology report describes a partial hepatectomy and cholecystectomy performed on a patient with hepatocellular carcinoma. The liver specimen weighs 630 grams and includes the left lobe and a portion of the right lobe. The tumor measures 10 x 9 x 7 cm and is well circumscribed. The tumor is described as having a firm, homogenous yellow-tan appearance. The uninvolved liver parenchyma and capsule are normal. Sections of the tumor and various sites are submitted for further analysis. 

The gallbladder specimen is also examined and shows no pathologic abnormalities. 

The final diagnosis is hepatocellular carcinoma with mixed sclerosing and adenoid patterns, with multifocal extension to the surgical margins. No vascular space invasion is identified.

The pathology report indicates that the patient underwent a partial hepatectomy (segment 4) and cholecystectomy for a well-defined mass (1.8 x 1.6 x 1.5 cm) in the liver that was suggestive of hepatocellular carcinoma. The gross type of the mass was nodular with perinodular extension, and there was no evidence of invasion in the portal vein or other areas. The tumor was found to be Edmondson-Steiner grade IV/IV and the histologic type was trabecular, pseudoglandular, compact with partial capsule formation and capsular infiltration. The major grade was II/IV. The gallbladder specimen indicated chronic cholecystitis and cholesterolosis. No other abnormalities were reported. The suggestion for this case is not specified.

The pathology report describes a left lateral sectorectomy of a liver specimen received for a patient with a preoperative diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma. A 3 cm tumor was found with moderately differentiated histologic type, invaded the capsule and visceral peritoneum, and extended into adjacent adhered omentum with hematoma and organization. The tumor is staged as pT4 due to visceral peritoneum invasion. Chronic hepatitis, grade 3 and stage 2, and capsular fibrosis with organizing hematoma and adhesions are also noted. Gross liver parenchymal margins were negative for tumor. The previous biopsy was correlated with the present findings.

The pathology report describes a case of hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient who underwent a lobectomy. The cancer appeared as a grossly nodular mass with nodular extension, and was found to have a sicrotrabecular histologic type and a haggate cell type. There was evidence of necrosis, hemorrhage, and fatty change, with partial fibrous capsule involvement and infiltration into the capsule. The cancer did not invade the portal vein, bile ducts, hepatic vein or artery, but there was microvascular invasion. There were no metastases, and the stage was reported as "oft". The report also noted chronic hepatitis, periportal fibrosis, and dysplasia in the ductal epithelia. Other findings included the presence of fatty change in the liver, and chronic cholecystitis in the gallbladder. Special stains were negative for iron and positive for cytokeratin 7 in the bile duct. A lump of adipose tissue was also examined.

The pathology report states that a well differentiated hepatocellular neoplasm was found in segments V and VI of the liver. The lesion is considered to be a grade 1 hepatocellular carcinoma due to its size, patient's age, and architectural pattern. Surgical margins were clear of involvement. The liver nodule measured 12 x 11 x 7.5 cm. The gallbladder, which was removed during surgery, showed chronic cholecystitis without any stones. A preliminary frozen section consultation suggests the possibility of either hepatocellular adenoma or grade 1 hepatocellular carcinoma.

The patient's pathology report indicates the presence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in the left lateral segment of the liver, with a moderately differentiated, multifocal tumor measuring 4.1 cm. The tumor has disrupted the liver capsule, showing signs of tumor extension. The biopsy taken during surgery shows architectural and cytologic atypia, but further analysis is needed to provide a definitive diagnosis. Mild steatosis and mild siderosis are also observed in the liver tissue. The full diagnosis and appropriate treatment plan require additional information and clinical correlation with the operative findings.

The pathology report describes a hepatocellular carcinoma in the right lobe of the liver, which was removed through a hepatectomy. The tumor was 10.5 x 8.0 x 7 cm in size and showed trabecular and pseudo-glandular histologic types with a classic and clear cell pattern. The tumor had partial capsule formation and infiltration, with septal formation present. There was no evidence of tumor necrosis, vascular invasion, or intrahepatic metastasis. The surgical margin was clear with no involvement of bile duct invasion, serosal invasion, or major branches of the hepatic vein. The pathologic stage was AJOG (p1) (p2). The report also mentions chronic hepatitis HBV-associated with minimal lobular activity, moderate portal-to-periportal activity, portal fibrosis, and chronic cholecystitis with cholesterosis of the gallbladder. Dysplasia and cirrhosis were absent.

The pathology report describes a 73-year-old female patient who underwent a cholecystectomy and partial hepatectomy. The analysis of the gallbladder specimen did not reveal any noteworthy findings. However, the partial hepatectomy specimen revealed a poorly differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma with multiple tumors located in the right hepatic lobe. The tumor had not invaded any vessels or lymph nodes, and the margins were uninvolved by carcinoma. The report also includes gross descriptions and additional pathological findings.

The pathology report describes the findings from a segmental resection of the liver's right lobe and en bloc resection of a liver tumor and gallbladder. The diagnosis is hepatocellular carcinoma, moderately differentiated, with 5% tumor necrosis. The gallbladder is also noted to have mid-chronic cholecystitis. The report indicates that the extent of primary tumor, regional lymph nodes, and distant metastasis cannot be assessed. The gross description of the specimens received is also provided.

The pathology report describes a liver resection of a segment 6 tumor diagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma. The tumor was found to be arising in micronodular cirrhosis and was completely excised with negative margins. The tumor size was 2.4 cm with no vascular invasion. The adjacent liver tissue showed moderate chronic inflammation and moderate to marked fixed hepatocellular steatosis. The tumor was graded as 2 on the Edmundson and Steiner scale and stage TI. A portion of the specimen was taken for research purposes.

The report describes a left lateral liver resection for a preoperative diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma. The postoperative diagnosis was also hepatocellular carcinoma. Multiple nodular masses ranging from 0.2 to 5.8 cm in size were found and were confined to the liver with no invasion into adjacent tissues. The histologic grade of the carcinoma was designated as well-differentiated. The report mentions that the margin of uninvolved tissue was 4mm from the invasive carcinoma. There was no evidence of vascular or perineural invasion. The report confirms the diagnosis of malignancy.

This pathology report describes the findings from a liver resection and cholecystectomy. The liver resection specimen shows a Grade 3 hepatocellular carcinoma, usual type, measuring 4.6 x 4.3 x 3.2 cm, with a single satellite nodule measuring 0.4 cm. The tumor is located in the right lobe of the liver and is not encapsulated. There is no evidence of extramural vascular invasion, and the surgical margins are free of tumor. The report also notes mild chronic cholecystitis in the gallbladder. The non-neoplastic liver shows mild tumor effect, but no evidence of chronic or primary liver disease is detected.

The pathology report is for a liver mass that was removed during a partial hepatectomy and cholecystectomy. The clinical diagnosis is suggested to be hepatocellular carcinoma. The gross appearance of the mass is well-defined, multinodular, solid, slightly firm, and without necrosis. The resection margin was not involved grossly, and there was periportal fibrosis (stage 2). Microscopic examination confirms the diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma, moderately differentiated with trabecular and pseudoglandular histologic types. The major differentiation is II, and the worst differentiation is III. The report also indicates the absence of invasion into the surgical resection margin, serosa, portal vein, microvessels, and intrahepatic metastasis. The gallbladder shows a chronic cholecystitis.

The pathology report describes the findings of a surgical procedure that included a cholecystectomy (removal of the gallbladder) and a right lobectomy (removal of the right lobe of the liver) due to a liver tumor. The tumor was found to be 9.5 cm in size and located 0.5 cm from the closest resection margin. The uninvolved liver parenchyma showed macrovesicular steatosis. The report includes details from the gross and microscopic analysis of the specimens submitted for evaluation and immunohistochemistry analyses.

The pathology report describes the findings of a surgical resection of a liver tumor in a patient with chronic hepatitis B and cirrhosis. Two segments of the liver were removed- segment #3 contained a large tumor (7.0 x 6.0 x 5.0 cm) with venous invasion and extensive tumor necrosis, while segment 4A and 8 contained a smaller tumor (1.5 x 1.0 x 1.0 cm) with no lymphovascular invasion and coming to within 2.0 mm of the blue-painted margin. The report also mentions soft necrotic areas within the larger tumor and no involvement of uninvolved liver parenchyma. The diagnosis is hepatocellular carcinoma with varying grades and extent, and the report notes the patient's hepatitis B and cirrhosis.

The liver tissue away from the tumor showed inflammation, fibrosis, and signs of necrosis and steatosis.

The pathology report describes a case of hepatocellular carcinoma in the left lateral segment of the liver. Immunohistochemistry stains revealed positive results for AFP, Hepatocyte paraffin 1, CEA-p, and antibodies CK7 and CK20. The tumor is classified as pT1, indicating a solitary tumor with no vascular invasion. Regional lymph nodes and distant metastasis could not be assessed. The margins of the resected liver tissue are uninvolved by invasive carcinoma, with a distance of 9 mm between the tumor and the closest margin. No venous invasion is observed. Additional findings include fibrous expansion of some portal areas with short fibrous septa. The gross description of the specimen confirms the presence of a 35 cm nodule within the liver tissue. The frozen section diagnosis confirmed the presence of the tumor and was communicated during the intraoperative consultation. The report also mentions the submission of tissue to the Tissue Procurement Laboratory.

This pathology report is for a patient who underwent surgery to remove a mass from their liver. The surgical specimen included the left lobe of the liver, a segment of the liver, needle biopsies from the liver, a lymph node, and the gallbladder.

The diagnosis for the left lobe of the liver excision is grade 3 hepatocellular carcinoma, which is a type of liver cancer. The tumor is described as multinodular and measures 25 x 16 x 9 cm. The tumor is contained within the liver, with no invasion into the surrounding tissues. The surgical margins are clear of tumor, with a clearance of 1.2 cm. The tumor is encapsulated by a fibrous capsule. Approximately 10% of the tumor shows necrosis. The adjacent non-neoplastic liver tissue does not show any abnormalities.

In the segment of the liver excision, grade 3 hepatocellular carcinoma is also diagnosed. The tumor measures 3 x 2 x 1.8 cm, and the margins are negative for tumor.

The needle biopsies from the liver reveal a hemangioma in biopsy #1 and no tumor in biopsy #2.

The lymph node excision shows a single benign lymph node.

The gallbladder removal did not show any diagnostic abnormalities.

An addendum to the report states that the adjacent non-neoplastic liver tissue does not show any abnormalities on permanent sections. Additional stains were negative.

Overall, the patient has grade 3 hepatocellular carcinoma in the liver, with no tumor invasion into surrounding tissues. The adjacent non-neoplastic liver tissue is normal, and the lymph node and gallbladder are also free of abnormalities.

The pathology report describes two specimens received - one from the gallbladder and the other a central hepatectomy section. The carcinoma is not reactive with antibodies CK20 and HSA, and extends focally to the hepatic resection line. There are also scattered bile duct hamartomas present. The synoptic report confirms a partially differentiated carcinoma, with lymphovascular invasion and involvement of the margin, but with no assessed regional lymph node metastasis or distant metastasis. Additional immunohistochemistry studies were conducted but not specified in the report. No clinical history is provided.

There was evidence of vascular invasion, but no bile duct invasion or serosal invasion was noted. A lymph node biopsy showed no tumor present. The report suggests a diagnosis of HCC with direct tumor extension to the gallbladder and the presence of lymphovascular emboli from the liver.

There is no normal stroma present within the biopsy tissue to exclude an invasive component, but stromal invasion is not definitively identified. The report was reviewed by an MD and a Dr. RAIAREENIHEI who concurs with the findings. The patient had astro apical andr cts on Pap smear, and a cervicotomy procedure was performed to obtain the biopsy material.

The pathology report indicates that a patient underwent a radical hysterectomy due to cervical cancer. The cancer was moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with some lymphovascular invasion identified. The tumor had not extended to the uterine corpus. Two tumors were identified. The report mentions the excision of several lymph nodes, all of which were benign and tested negative for cancer.

The pathology report describes the findings of a radical hysterectomy and salpingo-oophorectomy for a patient with invasive cervical carcinoma. The report notes that the right ovary had a follicular cyst and mild hyperplasia of rete elements, while the right fallopian tube had minimal chronic inflammation and inflammatory cell aggregates; the left ovary had serosal adhesions, and the left fallopian tube had minimal chronic inflammation, inflammatory cell accumulations, focal epithelial hyperplasia, and paratubal cystic Walthard rests. Four reactive lymph nodes from the right pelvic, one lymph node from the right periaortic, ten lymph nodes from the left pelvic, one lymph node from the left common iliac, and six reactive lymph nodes from the left obturator showed no evidence of metastatic carcinoma. One of four parametrial lymph nodes contained metastatic carcinoma on the left side. The uterus had poorly differentiated primary invasive cervical carcinoma with predominantly squamous cell features, associated squamous cell carcinoma in situ, lymphatic and blood vessel invasion in the cervix, lymphatic invasion in the left paranetrium, and without direct extension of carcinoma into parametrial soft tissues. There was no extension of carcinoma into the uterine corpus, but the tumor had fibrosing stromal reaction and was partially ulcerated and necrotic. Two uterine leiomyomas were also noted, along with benign inactive endometrium.

The pathology report describes a case of invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, which is poorly differentiated and measures 6.5 cm. There is evidence of vascular invasion and the carcinoma extends to the cervical cuff margin. Regional lymph nodes are affected with metastatic carcinoma present in one right and one left pelvic lymph node. The left periaortic lymph nodes demonstrate no evidence of metastasis. There is no distant metastasis seen in the specimen and no other findings reported.

The pathology report describes a fresh frozen tumor sample that was obtained from a 63-year-old patient's cervix during a surgical resection. The tumor was found to be a nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma with possible lymphovascular invasion and a tumor size of 2.9 cm. Pathological staging revealed T1b, N1 (with 1 out of 23 sampled nodes being positive), and M0. The tumor was graded 3/3 and all resection margins were clear.
The pathology report indicates that the primary site for examination was the cervix. The biopsy results show an infiltrative poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

The pathology report indicates that the primary site of the tumor is in the cervix. The tumor is a mucinous adenocarcinoma of the endocervical type, with a histologic grade 2. It has infiltrated the deep third of the cervical wall, with a depth of 8.0 mm and an extension of 35 mm. The margins around the tumor are not involved. The neoplasia has not spread to the parametria, uterine tubes, ovaries, or pelvic lymph nodes. The report is dated 3/7/14.

The patient underwent a radical hysterectomy, bilateral salpingectomy, and parametrectomy for cervical cancer. The tumor was a well-differentiated endocervical adenocarcinoma that involved the cervix circumferentially, including the endocervix, with an extent of invasion of the outer half and a depth of 8mm; the tumor size was 2.5cm. There was no involvement of the deep margin, lower uterine segment, or parametrium, and the cervical/vaginal margin was free of tumor. Lymphovascular space invasion was absent, and none of the 20 examined lymph nodes showed involvement. The Fallopian tubes had no tumor, and there was also no significant pathologic abnormality in the myometrium. The final pathologic stage was pT1b1 pNO pMx.

The pathology report contains information on the collection of cancerous tissue from a patient. The report includes the patient's clinical information, past medical history, medications, diagnostic studies, surgical treatment, and pathology report. The pathology report displays the organ, size, extension of tumor, lymph nodes, metastasis, and the histological pattern of the tumor. Additionally, the report includes details on cell distribution, structural pattern, and cellular differentiation. The report shows a clinical diagnosis of cancer and gives the pathological staging as pT N M Stage: zLlb.

The pathology report describes the results of a cervical biopsy of a female patient with a personal history of cancer. The biopsy revealed invasive moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with features of in situ adenocarcinoma and a focal tumor cell necrosis, which was positive for p16, CK-7, and CEA-nonoclonal but negative for Calretinin, CD 10, and CK-20. An endocervical mass biopsy confirmed the presence of invasive and in situ endocervical adenocarcinoma with mucinous features. The report also mentions endometrial curettings showing proliferative-type endometrium with no malignancy detected. The report includes a disclaimer regarding immunohistochemistry tests and the absence of necessary clearance or approval from the appropriate authorities.
The pathology report states that the primary site is the cervix. The biopsy reveals invasive poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

The pathology report describes a specimen that consists of the uterus and left fallopian tube. The uterus and fallopian tube appear abnormal upon examination. There is a hard and ulcerated lesion in the cervix that measures 3.4 x 3.0 cm in size. Multiple round, firm, and whitish lesions are also seen in the myometrium (muscular wall of the uterus). Microscopic examination confirms the presence of invasive squamous cell carcinoma, a type of cervical cancer. The tumor has infiltrated the surrounding tissue to a depth of 1.38 cm and extends horizontally for 2.8 cm. The uterine isthmus and margins of resection are not involved. There is also evidence of an extensive component of squamous cell carcinoma in situ (pre-cancerous cells). Neoplastic lymphatic embolization is present, indicating spread of cancer via the lymphatic system. Additionally, uterine leiomyomas (benign growths in the uterus), endometriosis in the parametrium (tissue surrounding the uterus), and the left fallopian tube are observed. The endometrium (lining of the uterus) shows signs of dysfunction with moderate stromal edema. The pathological staging indicates stage pT1b1 and pN1 according to the TNM 7th edition staging system.

The pathology report describes a lymph node and adipose tissue specimen received for lymphoma workup. The diagnosis reveals a highly proliferative diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with a histiocyte-rich background. On immunoassays, the lymphoma is positive for CD20, bel-2 and MUN-1, negative to weakly positive for bcl6, negative for CD10 and CD30, and with a Ki-67 proliferation index of 60-95%. The report notes a prominent background of T cells and a florid proliferation of reactive histiocytes. No clinical history is given, but the pre-operative diagnosis was lymphadenopathy.

The pathology report describes a patient with cervical lymphadenopathy and skin lesions. One lymph node from the left side was excised and found to have reactive hyperplasia and benign salivary gland tissue, while a lymph node from the left deep level 2 had diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The report also describes a right skin lesion which showed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Further molecular and cytogenetic studies were performed on the specimens. Immunohistochemical studies indicated a reactive phenotype.

The pathology report describes a biopsy of an inguinal lymph node that shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which is positive for CD20, BCL2, BCL6, and IgD. The atypical cells have Kappa light chain restriction and are negative for CD10 and MUM1. The report also notes a Ki-67 proliferative index of 50-60% and a rearrangement in the BCL2 gene. No further information is provided about the size or characteristics of any other lymph nodes.

The report describes a biopsy and resection of a mass in the cerebellopontine angle, which was found to be a Diffuse Large Cell B-Cell Lymphoma of the follicular center cell type. The tumor cells are atypical, with hyperchromatic nuclei and significant cytologic atypia. Foci of tumor necrosis and numerous mitotic figures are seen. The tumor cells are positive for CD45 and CD20, and negative for keratin AE1 AE3, CD3, CD30, and BCL2. The immunophenotype of the tumor is CD45+, CD20+, CD10+, MUM-1+, BCL6+, CD3-, CD43-, CD30-, BCL2-. A final diagnosis will be issued pending review of additional stains and hematopathology consultation.

The pathology report describes a poorly preserved tumor in the left submandibular (salivary) gland and fibrofatty connective tissues. The tumor is consistent with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The frozen section diagnosis confirms infiltration of the salivary gland by undifferentiated tumor cells. The gross description reveals normal appearance of the cut sections of the submandibular gland with no visible solid nodules. The microscopic description confirms fibrofatty connective tissue infiltrated by malignant tumor cells with degenerate cells and scattered pyknotic nuclear debris present. Inmunostains demonstrate the lesional cells to be positive with CD10, bel-6, MUM-1, and CD20, while Cyclin D1, Td?, bel2, AE1/3, and $100 are negative. Mild chronic inflammation is present in some areas. No dendritic meshworks are identified. A separate fragment of normal thymus is also present.

The pathology report indicates that the patient had a brainstem tumor, specifically diffuse large cell lymphoma of B-cell type. The microscopic description shows poorly cohesive, large cells with multiple nucleoli and numerous mitotic figures. The tumor has an angiocentric pattern and areas of glial and fibrous scarring. The neoplastic cells are immunoreactive for CD5 and CD20, confirming B-cell lymphocytic origin, and demonstrate aberrant expression of the T-cell marker CD43. They are negative for GFAP, S-100, cytokeratin 8/18, CD3, and CD45. Overall, the immunophenotype is consistent with a diffuse large cell B-cell lymphoma.

The report describes a surgical resection of the terminal ileum and right colon. A mass was found in the region of the ileocecal valve and cecum, which was infiltrative and ulcerated and extended through the wall. The mass was found to be a B-cell lymphoma involving the full thickness of the affected area. The lymphoma was CD5 positive and the immunohistochemical stains showed the tumor cells to be positive for BCL-6, CD23, CD5, and PAXS. Cyclin D1, MUM-1, CD10, CD3, and CD43 were negative. The differential diagnosis was between CD5 positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma versus an atypical mantle cell lymphoma. Tissue was sent for studies for the t(11;14) translocation to help clarify the diagnosis, and results of FISH studies will be reported in an addendum when available. No tumor was seen in the lymph nodes.

The pathology report shows a final diagnosis of a lymph node with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, non-cleaved. The tumor cells have a germinal center B-cell phenotype. Immunohistochemistry and molecular diagnostic studies were performed to confirm the B-cell phenotype. The specimen was entirely submitted according to the lymphoma study group protocol. The frozen and fixed tissue samples were used for further research and testing. The paraffin markers indicate a B-cell phenotype. The report also includes information about the patient's clinical history and pre- and post-operative diagnoses.

The pathology report describes a tissue fragment of a lymph node in the axillary region of the body that measures 7x5.3x4.3 cm, containing 4x43.4 cm lymph node with a pinky color and a 3.8x3.3 cm whitish area. Three other lymph nodes of pinky color are also observed, measuring 2.5x2.3x2.2 cm. The left axillary lymph node excision reveals diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with high proliferative index, which is positive for CD20, BCL6, and p53, negative for BCL2, CD10, and MUM. It also shows a scarce presence of intratumoral reactive T-cells with a KI67 proliferative index of 70%. The associated lymph nodes show reactive follicular hyperplasia. No rearrangement of the BCL2 gene by PCR (MBR) has been observed.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the stomach consisting of small-sized cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and with diffuse growth up to 5.5 cm. The tumor has replaced the gastric mucosa and spread to the muscular layer, but there is no invasion present. The report recommends IHC-stainings as the case is consistent with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Additionally, there is a second conclusion of a tumor consisting of middle-sized lymphoid cells with some regions containing large atypical cells, consistent with a marginal zone B-cell lymphoma. The lymph nodes tested negative for metastasis, and there is no evidence of neo-adjuvant treatment. The report does not provide information on tumor extent, grade, or margins.

The pathology report indicates that the specimen taken from the spleen is diagnosed with malignant lymphoma, NOS (not otherwise specified). The report also includes details about the tissue structure and cells present in the specimen. It mentions the presence of low-grade abnormal cells with increased reticulin and collagen proportion. However, the report also indicates that there is no evidence of lymphoma in the sample. Additional biopsies from the right and left iliac crest are mentioned, but there is no information about their results.

The pathology report describes the excised lymph node from the left neck of a female patient with suspected lymphoma. The final diagnosis is non-cleaved diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL-NC), which is consistent with a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder. The immunophenotype of the lymphoma is non-GCB type and is characterized by the increased expression of CD19, CD20, partial CD25, high-density CD38, and monotypic, intermediate density lambda light chains. Further testing including flow cytometry, cytogenetic studies, and immunohistochemistry were done to confirm the diagnosis. The report stresses that clinical diagnosis and therapy for the patient should not solely depend on this assay.

The pathology report describes an orchiectomy specimen weighing 832.1 grams with a well-defined solid tumor representing 90% of the testicular volume. The tumor is identified as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with a high proliferative index. The histological examination shows the tumor consists of large atypical immunoblastic cells which have replaced the majority of the testicular parenchyma, with extensive areas of necrosis. The tumor is positive for CD20, CD79a, BCL2, MUM1, Kappa light chain restriction and has a proliferation index of 100%. There is a very scarce intratumoral T-cell infiltration.

The pathology report indicates the presence of diffuse large cell malignant lymphoma in the left cervical neck lymph node. The report also includes results from a bone marrow biopsy that show orderly hemopoiesis and no evidence of lymphoma involvement but dysplasia present in the myeloid and erythroid series. The report recommends reviewing the flow cytometry immunophenotypic report for further information.

The pathology report describes a left iliac mass that was excised and identified as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, anaplastic type. The tumor had large and pleomorphic cells with a high mitotic rate. The patient had a history of a left hemipelvis lesion. Immunohistochemical studies revealed a B-cell phenotype, with germinal center B-cell phenotype demonstrated. The report also includes information on various tests performed on the specimen, including an immunoperoxidase report and special requests made by the ordering and referring physicians. The report also mentions other possible diagnoses, including monoclonal B-cell lymphoma, surface Ig negative B-cell lymphoma, peripheral T-cell lymphoma, Hodgkin's disease, and null phenotype.

The pathology report describes two lymph nodes measuring 2x1.4cm and cm in size that appear soft and hyperemic. The report suggests Non-Hodgkin's Large B-cell lymphoma with partial lesion of adjacent lymph node, which was probably localized on the side of malignant process. The tumor cells did not react with melanosome (HMB-45) or chromogranin A (DAK-A3) but reacted positively with CD 45 (PD7/26), CD 20cy (L26), and CD 10 (56C6) in follicular centers. Ki67 Protein (MIB-1) also showed a high percentage of up to 40% in tumor cells. The diagnosis is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the lymph node with unspecified grade and uninvolved margins. Venous invasion is absent, and the extent of the tumor is unspecified.

The pathology report describes a lymph node excision that reveals the presence of a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with centroblastic morphology. The tumor population is positive for CD20, CD79a CD10, BCL6, and CD23, and negative for CD3, CDS, BCL2, CD21, and p53. A Lambda light chain restriction is observed, and there are abundant reactive T-cells positive for CD3 and CDS. The Ki-67 proliferation index is 75%. The FISH study has shown gains of the BCL-6 gene and losses of chromosome 1 (region 1p36), but no rearrangements of the BCL2 gene.

The pathology report describes a diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in a piece of a left level 2 cervical lymph node, which was found to have a patternless mass of medium-sized cells with ample, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and irregular, vesicular nuclei containing dispersed chromatin. The lymphoma was positive for pan-B cell marker CD20 and coexpresses late-to-postgerminal center-associated MUM1 with germinal center-associated protein BCL6, as well as antiapoptosis protein BCL-2. It is largely negative for germinal center-associated antigen CD10, which excludes Burkitt lymphoma, and negative for Cyclin D1, ruling out blastoid mantle cell lymphoma. There is no evidence of a metastatic malignancy or granulomas. The report notes that external positive controls are in working order.

The report describes a pathological examination of a lymph node in the right submaxillary region. The lymph node is found to be completely replaced with a diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphoid proliferation, indicating the presence of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The tumor is also associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection. There are areas of necrosis and fibrosis, and an angiocentric growth pattern is observed. The tumor cells show positivity for CD20, CD79a, OCT-2, BOB.1, BCL2, MUMI, LMP1, and CD30, and negativity for CD10, BCL6, CD15, ALK1, CD3, CD4, CDS, CD7, and D8. The Ki67 proliferative index is high (70%). Additional testing using PCR reveals a monoclonal population of cells with IGH FR3 and a polyclonal population with TCR gamma.

The pathology report describes the biopsy of a mediastinal mass and paratracheal lymph node. The diagnosis is a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in the mediastinal mass and reactive hyperplasia in the lymph node. The tumor is high-grade and has a vaguely nodular-to-diffuse architecture with fibrovascular partitioning and focal necrosis. The tumor cells are diffusely positive for pan-B cell marker CD20, with intense immunoreactivity for germinal center-associated transcription modulator bel-6, widespread coexpression of late-to-post-germinal center-associated transcription factor MUM-1 as well as anti-apoptosis protein bel-2. The diagnosis remains unchanged even with the inadvertently omitted immunohistochemical result.

The pathology report describes an enlarged lymph node with a size of 1.5x1 cm, with a soft, dark brown and gray surface. Microscopically, the tumor architectures are replaced by a diffuse pattern composed of small or enlarged transformed lymphoid cells with irregular hyperchromatic nuclei. The tumor cells are oval or round in shape with scant cytoplasm and single or multiple nucleoli. Mitotic figures are common. The diagnosis is malignant lymphoma, large B-cell, diffuse type. Tumor markers CD20(+) and CD3(-) were also observed.

The pathology report includes specimens from multiple lymph nodes and lung biopsies taken from the patient with a lung mass. Six out of the seven lymph nodes biopsied were negative for malignancy, whereas the right proximal paratracheal biopsy (G) showed malignant lymphoma, specifically diffuse large cell type histiocytic-rich. The lung biopsy on the anterior segment of the right upper lobe (H) showed respiratory mucosa with focal squamous metaplasia and chronic inflammation. An immunohistochemical study showed that the malignant cells from the right proximal paratracheal biopsy were positive for CO20 and CD10 and negative for other markers. Additionally, there were two specimens, a bone marrow biopsy/aspirate (A) and (B), with no diagnostic information provided in the summary.

The pathology report describes a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in the small intestine and sigmoid colon. The tumor mass measures 15 x 14 x 5 cm and displays a "starry sky" appearance with neoplastic B-cell lymphoid cells expressing CD20, PAKS, and germinal center markers. The phenotype is consistent with the germinal center B-cell (GCB) type by Hans' criteria, but also shows weak immunostaining for MUMI and strong immunoreactivity for FoxPl, which are more characteristic of the activated B-cell (ABC) subtype. There is no evidence of Burkitt lymphoma.

The pathology report describes a sample of colonic tissue measuring 0.2cm to 0.5cm in greatest dimension. Microscopic examination reveals infiltrating sheets of intermediate to large malignant cells consistent with large B cell lymphoma. Immunohistochemical studies were conducted, showing positivity for Bel-2, Bel-6, and MUN 1, and high MIB-1 expression (greater than 80% of lesional cells). The diagnosis is malignant lymphoma, consistent with large B cell lymphoma.

The report describes a solid tumor in the breast measuring 4x3x3.5 cm with invasion of benign breast tissue. The tumor is identified as Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma, a poorly differentiated type with large transformed lymphoid cells. No lymph nodes were found to be positive for metastasis. Other details, including the Nottingham Histologic Score, margins, and evidence of neo-adjuvant treatment, are not specified.

The pathology report shows a diagnosis of malignant lymphoma, large B cell, diffuse type located in the small intestine (jejunum) with invasion and ulceration of the tumor. The tumor cells are composed of large transformed lymphoid cells and multinuclei giant cells and are positive for CD20 and negative for CD3 and CKAE1/AE3. Lymph nodes in the mesentery were not affected.

The report describes a large mass found in the left inguinal lymph node which has been identified as Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma. The tumor is made up of abnormal large cells of the centroblastic type, with a high Ki67 proliferation index. Immunohistochemistry has confirmed positivity for CD20, CD79a, CD10, bel-6, and bel-2, and negativity for MUM1. The report further states that FISH testing has found a MYC gene rearrangement.

The pathology report indicates that the patient has primary mediastinal diffuse large B cell lymphoma, which has spread to the axillary lymph nodes. The lymph node shows a diffuse growth pattern composed of anaplastic cells with sclerosis. The immunophenotypic study shows that the neoplastic cells are positive for CD20, CD79a, BOB1, OCT2, BCL2, and BCL6 with moderate and heterogeneous expression of CD30, and negative for CD10, CD3, CD5, and CD15. The Ki-67 proliferative index is 90%, indicating a high rate of cell division. In situ hybridization for Epstein-Barr virus is negative.

The pathology report describes a surgical biopsy of a patient's thyroid gland. The diagnosis shows evidence of lymphoma, a type of cancer that affects the lymphatic system. The sample was prepared for further study using cytogenetics and molecular testing, and additional data such as the patient's medical history and related conditions are also included. The report concludes with the signature of the responsible pathologist.

The pathology report describes a cervical lymph node excision revealing primary mediastinal diffuse large B cell lymphoma. The neoplastic cells have atypical large cells with immunoblastic and Reed-Sternberg morphology. The cells are positive for CD20, PAXS, and partially for CD30 and CD23, negative for CD15, and have a Ki67 proliferation index of 40%. In situ hybridization for the Epstein-Barr virus (EBER) was negative. Several reactive T-cells are observed.

The pathology report indicates the presence of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in enlarged lymph nodes with multifocal dissemination, including extranodal involvement in the liver and spleen. There is no evidence of venous invasion or involvement of margins. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) stainings revealed positive reactions to CD45 and CD20 and negative reactions to CD3 in tumor cells with positive reactions on reactive cells. Some tumor cells showed positive reactions to CD30. Five out of five lymph nodes tested were positive.

The pathology report describes enlarged lymph nodes with a soft, yellowish, and gray surface. Microscopic examination shows irregular lymphoid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei in a diffuse pattern intermixed with macrophages. The tumor is composed of large B cells with scant cytoplasm and multiple nucleoli. Mitotic figures are common. The diagnosis is malignant lymphoma, large B cell, diffuse type. The tumor is located in bilateral cervical lymph nodes and measures 1 to 1.5 cm. Tumor markers include CD20 and negative CD3.

The report describes a biopsy of a supraclavicular lymph node that reveals a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Immunoprofiling shows that the tumor cells are positive for CD20 and CD79a, negative for cyclin D1, CD5, and CD10. The Ki 67/MIBL activity is high (80-90%). The amended diagnosis is Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL). The biopsy also shows areas of geographic necrosis.

The pathology report contains the findings for four specimens: a right groin lymph node excision, left fallopian tube and ovary, a right ovarian cyst excision, and a mesenteric mass biopsy. The diagnosis for the right groin lymph node excision is diffuse large B cell lymphoma, while the left fallopian tube and ovary are benign. The right ovarian cyst is a corpus luteum cyst. The mesenteric mass biopsy is also diagnosed as diffuse large B cell lymphoma. The report includes microscopic descriptions and immunoperoxidase stains. Flow cytometry analysis showed a neoplastic B cell population expressing certain markers. Further tests are recommended on the lymphoma tissue sections.

The pathology report describes a large B-cell lymphoma, grade 3a, located in the right thyroid mass. The lymphoma is based on CD21-inmunoreactive follicular dendritic meshworks and is diffusely positive for pan-B cell marker CD20. The cell proliferation fraction is uniform around 70-80% by Ki-67 immunolabelling. There is an intermingled, diminutive centrocytic component discernible focally, in keeping with a component of WHO Grade 3A follicular lymphoma. The report rules out Burkitt's lymphoma. The lymphoma is negative for cyclin Di, except for physiological expression in scattered thyrofollicular epithelial, histiocytic, and activated endothelial nuclei, which excludes a transformed mantle cell lymphoma. The report also notes a background of lymphocytic thyroiditis and fibrosis.

The pathology report describes a case of diffuse large cell lymphoma of the stomach with metastases in the lymph nodes of omentum minor and segment III of liver. The tumor in the stomach measured 10x8 cm with invasion into the muscular layer and showed infiltration by medium and large cells of lymphoid origin. The cells were positive for CD20 and Ki-67=60% by immunohistochemistry.

The pathology report indicates that there are three tissue fragments of a cervical lymph node. The left cervical lymph node excision shows a primary mediastinal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, with atypical lymphoid proliferation composed of sheets of large and pleomorphic cells with Reed-Sternberg morphology. The neoplastic cells are positive for several markers, including CD20, CD30, and MUMI/IRF4. There is a moderate amount of reactive T-cells. The Ki67 proliferative index is 70-80%, and there is a normal karyotype.

The pathology report describes two specimens, one from a left cervical level 5 lymph node and another from bone marrow. The lymph node biopsy shows malignant lymphoma, diffuse, large cell type, B-cell phenotype with a preliminary flow cytometric report indicating the lymphoma cells are positive for CD19, CD20, and CD22. Frozen section diagnosis confirms malignant lymphoma. The bone marrow biopsy shows orderly hematopoiesis and is negative for lymphoma. There is no dysplasia observed in either biopsy. The bone marrow samples were taken from the right and left ilac crest, with an average cellularity of 35%.

The pathology report describes a lymph node that is 3x3x3cm in size, located intra-abdominally, and has a soft, yellowish and gray surface. The tumor cells are composed of small and large transformed lymphoid cells with irregular hyperchromatic nuclei, oval or round in shape with scant cytoplasm, and multiple nucleoli. Mitotic figures are common. The diagnosis is malignant lymphoma, large B cell, diffuse type, and the histologic grade is poorly differentiated. There is evidence of CD20 and CD3 expression. No information is provided on neo-adjuvant treatment or treatment effect severity.

The pathology report refers to the examination of two specimens, an omental biopsy and mesenteric nodules. The intraoperative consultation diagnosis suggests the presence of pleomorphic B-linage lymphoma. The microscopic description confirms the occurrence of large pleomorphic B-linage lymphoma consistent with T-cell histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma in both the specimens. Immunohistochemistry and special staining reveal certain negative and positive markers that support the diagnosis of T-cell histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma as favored by the doctor. No clinical history of the patient is given, and the pre-operative diagnosis is intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy.

The lymph node is enlarged and has a smooth, whitish surface. The biopsy result shows a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with focal plasmocellular differentiation. Immunohistochemical study shows positive for CD20, CD79a, CD43 BCL2, BCL6, and MUM1 and negative for CD3, CDS, CD10, CD23, CD21, and p53. The cells show kappa light chain restriction and a Ki67 proliferation index of approximately 60%. No rearrangement of the BCL2 gene has been observed. Further testing and treatment may be necessary.

The pathology report describes the presence of a Subgaleal Mass C47, which was identified as a Large Cell Lymphoma, B-Cell Type. The lymphoma was of probable follicular center cell origin and was confirmed by immunoreactivity for CD45, CD20, and vimentin. The tumor cells were negative for cytokeratin, CD99, desmin, synaptophysin, S-100, and CD34. The microscopic description revealed large, non-cohesive cells with nuclei that ranged from open to hyperchromatic, and scattered mitotic figures were seen. Overall, the diagnosis was a B-cell lymphoma.

The pathology report describes the diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in the left cervical lymph node of a 60-year-old male patient, with a germinal center cell phenotype. The report also includes an immunoperoxidase report indicating a B-cell phenotype.

The pathology report describes a tumor in the small intestine that is moderately-margin, soft, solid, or yellow-gray in color with a size of 6x5x3cm. There are also three mesenteric masses measuring 0.5x2cm. The microscopic description reveals that the mucosa is ulcerated, and the tumor cells are large transformed lymphoid cells with hyperchromatic enlarged nuclei and defined cytoplasm. The diagnosis is Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the small intestine. The IHC results show that CD20 is positive, CD3 and CKAE1/AE3 are negative. There is also extranodal involvement of the small intestine and mesenteric lymph nodes. There is no neo-adjuvant treatment and there are no additional comments.

The pathology report indicates that the patient has Cholangiocarcinoma, a type of cancer that affects the bile ducts, in the right lobe of the liver. The tumor is multifocal and the largest focus is 3.3 cm in size. There is no evidence of cirrhosis in the tumor, but the uninvolved liver is evolving with focal hepatocellular differentiation consistent with cirrhosis. Immunohistochemical stains show that the malignant cells are positive for C7 but negative for hepatocellular markers. The report also indicates that there is evidence of moderately differentiated invasive carcinoma identified with tumor extension confined to hepatic parenchyma. The margins of the resection are uninvolved by invasive carcinoma except for the parenchymal margin, which is involved by 1 mm. The primary tumor status is multiple, and the number of nodes involved and examined is 0. Consultation of the liver tumor and biopsy is also provided in the report.

The pathology report indicates that the patient had a partially resected liver tumor, which was found to be a combination of cholangiocarcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. The tumor was moderately to poorly differentiated and had a maximum size of 3-5cm. Vascular invasion was identified for the carcinoma but could not be assessed for large or small vessels. The non-neoplastic liver showed features compatible with chronic viral hepatitis B and multiple von Meyenburg complexes (bile duct hamartomas). The diagnosis was based on histological and immunophenotypic findings, and the significance of the von Meyenburg complexes regarding potential causality for (or contribution to) neoplasia is unclear in the pathology literature. There was no evidence of distant metastasis, and the regional lymph nodes could not be assessed. Ancillary studies such as immunohistochemistry were performed to determine the epithelial markers for the neoplastic cells. The clinical history indicated that the patient had hepatitis B infection. The report includes gross description, specimen container labeling, and other relevant information.

The pathology report indicates that during surgery, a mass measuring 6.8 x 6.6 x 5.8 cm was found in the liver, specifically in segments V and VI. The tumor was identified as grade 2 intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and had multiple lobules. The tumor was closely located to the surgical resection margin, being only 0.3 cm away. No other significant findings are noted in the report.

The pathology report includes the findings of a liver excision and partial hepatectomy. The liver excision showed hemorrhage and mild steatosis, but no tumor. The partial hepatectomy showed a cholangiocarcinoma, a mass forming subtype, with a grade 2 of 4 (moderately differentiated) and a tumor size of 11.9 cm. The tumor had no perineural or capsular invasion but was focally suspicious for lymphovascular invasion. The margins were negative, and no lymph nodes were identified. The background liver showed mild steatosis and minimal non-specific portal chronic inflammation. The cholecystectomy showed chronic cholecystitis, with no dysplasia or carcinoma identified. The report is subject to change based on clinical review and additional information.

The pathology report describes a 9.0 x 6.5 x 5.8 cm mass consistent with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma that was found in the liver's right lobe and caudate lobe. The tumor is grade 3 (of 4) and is present at the surgical resection margin. The gallbladder showed no diagnostic abnormalities, and a single pericholedochal lymph node did not have any tumors. Immunohistochemical stains were reactive for CK7 and background staining with COX2 but lacked staining for CK20, TTF-1, chromogranin, and synaptophysin.

The report describes the findings of a liver and gallbladder resection that showed invasive grade 3 cholangiocarcinoma, forming a mass at the hilar region of the gallbladder. PART 3: Tumor thrombus excision - Sarcomatoid carcinoma with necrosis.

PART 4: Left kidney, spleen, tail of pancreas, and associated soft tissue resection - High-grade, partially cystic, partially sarcomatoid carcinoma, favor dedifferentiated renal cell carcinoma. Possible small clear cell carcinomatous component present. Carcinoma involves the upper pole of the kidney, perirenal adipose tissue, Gerota's fascia, tail of pancreas, and retroperitoneal soft tissue. Large occlusive tumor thrombus present in the main renal vein, extending to the renal vein surgical resection margin. Small vessel angiolymphatic invasion also identified. Brisk host lymphocytic reaction observed. Benign ureter, spleen, accessory spleen, and six renal and perisplenic lymph nodes. Carcinoma present at the main renal vein surgical resection margin and Gerota's fascia resection margin. All other surgical resection margins are benign. Pathologic stage assumed as pT4 Nx Mx; G4.

PART 6: Left psoas muscle excision - Sarcomatoid carcinoma infiltrating skeletal muscle.

The report also includes an evaluation of the non-neoplastic renal parenchyma, which showed changes consistent with early diabetic nephropathy, such as diffuse mesangial expansion with focal nodular glomerulosclerosis. There was also extensive global glomerulosclerosis and severe vascular scarring. These changes are seen in patients with diabetic kidney disease, although they can also result from other causes such as inherited or acquired procoagulant states, certain drugs, or radiation.

The microscopic examination of the kidney tissue revealed thickened basement membranes of the glomerular capillary walls, occasional double contours, and mild mononuclear inflammatory infiltration in the interstitium. Approximately 40% of the tissue showed tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis. The arteries and arterioles showed severe sclerosis and narrowing of the lumen.

The report does not mention any operative findings or provide a clinical diagnosis.
